detail.abstract: An action can be governed correctly and still be unprovable. This is the gap this paper addresses. An Execution Governance Kernel (EGK) operating at an execution boundary can evaluate a proposed action, apply a compiled standard, and reach a determination-permit or deny- with total fidelity. It can do this every time, deterministically, before the action commits. None of that is in question here. What is in question is what happens next: the kernel's own record of what it decided is produced by the same system whose behavior that record is meant to prove. A determination that can only be verified by asking the party who made it is not evidence. It is testimony from an interested party, and every institution that has ever priced risk, adjudicated liability, or underwritten a loss has already refused to accept that kind of testimony as sufficient.

detail.abstract: Organizations invest heavily in artificial intelligence without realizing the expected gains in intelligence and productivity. This paper traces that pattern to a problem of architecture and proposes an integrative theoretical framework that treats the organization as a hybrid cognitive system. Its core proposition is: organizational intelligence does not arise in individual actors, but in the quality with which an organization couples the necessary cognitive functions into a closed loop. Organizational intelligence is accordingly defined as the quality with which an organization continuously closes the cognition cycle Perceiving → Interpreting → Deciding → AcƟng → Learning under uncertainty-substrate-neutrally, that is, regardless of whether humans or AI systems perform the functions. Intelligence resides in the transitions, not in the stations; organizational stupidity becomes diagnosable as a locatable interruption of the loop. The proposed mechanism is the cognitive economy: cognition cycles organize around their scarcest cognitive resource; AI shifts that scarcity from information processing to collective, accountable judgment formation under uncertainty, and thereby forces the organization to reconfigure. That scarcity migrates is presented as a derivation, not merely an observation. A law of the minimum bounds attainable intelligence by the weakest coupling among four architectural layers (cognitive, social, accountability, technological); it is derived as a consequence of the transition thesis under an explicitly stated simultaneity premise. A fractal thesis extends the framework-as a working hypothesis-to nested loops across organizational levels. The framework is delimited against cycle predecessors (OODA, PDCA, Kolb), distributed cognition (Hutchins; Clark & Chalmers; Weick & Roberts) and organization-theoretic relatives (Galbraith, Ocasio, Teece, Beer, Malone, Senge; Milgrom & Roberts; Kremer), translated into falsifiable predictions, and made operationalizable through four measures of loop closure. The claim advanced is that of a theoretical integration framework, not that of a new general theory of organization.

title: Artificial Intelligence: Supply-Chain Chokepoints and the Reach of Industrial Policy

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence: Supply-Chain Chokepoints and the Reach of Industrial Policy
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence depends on a stack of inputs, models on compute, compute on chips, and chips on electricity and refined minerals. This paper measures the concentration of each layer on one scale, the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI), from cited and reproducible data. Three findings follow. First, concentration forms a clear gradient. It is modest downstream, where public and regulatory attention is heaviest and model usage and cloud fall below the 1,800 mark United States agencies treat as highly concentrated. It rises steeply upstream, where public discourse is sparse. There advanced packaging scores 8,100, leading-edge lithography reaches the ceiling of 10,000, and one country dominates the production or refining of several critical minerals, gallium near that maximum. Second, these upstream layers are chokepoints and a strategic vulnerability for the whole AI economy. Antitrust cannot reach them, because they lie in foreign or state hands. Contesting them falls to export controls and domestic industrial policy. Third, placing reserves beside refining shows the concentration is built rather than geological, a variable industrial policy can move. A rise in an upstream input's price barely changes the cost of the product built from it, because the input is only a small share of that cost. A chokepoint's threat is therefore the loss of the input itself rather than a higher price.

title: Unbundling Cloud Residency and ERP Replacement: A Constructed Case in Capital Allocation and Decision Governance

detail.title: Unbundling Cloud Residency and ERP Replacement: A Constructed Case in Capital Allocation and Decision Governance

detail.abstract:
A 250-employee Tier-1 supplier of keyboard subassemblies in Medley, Florida, with $62.5 million of revenue and 71 percent of that revenue in three customers, must decide whether to renew its public-cloud commitments, repatriate its infrastructure while retaining its enterprise resource planning system, or execute a full sovereign build on-premises. QWERTY, Inc. is constructed: every figure is stipulated and falls inside ranges computed from the FY2025 filings of five electronics-manufacturing comparables. The case is presented as the documents that decided it, with the model’s worksheets appended so that any material figure may be traced to its stated input and method.

The central finding is a separation. The choice as it reached the chief executive bundled two decisions — where the firm’s computing should reside, and which enterprise system it should run — with different timescales, reversibility, capital profiles and customer risk. Unbundled, they point in opposite directions. Repatriating the infrastructure saves $1,281,000 over five years for $451,021 of capital, pays back in 24.0 months and reverses in three. Replacing the enterprise system does not pay back within five years under any deployment costed.

What carries the decision is contractual rather than economic. Exit cost runs $192,000 under selective repatriation against $1,971,000 under the sovereign build, at a firm where losing either of two customers breaches a leverage covenant in the first year and where the sole measure addressing customer concentration draws on that same facility. Vendor lifecycle risk, exposed only by naming candidates, eliminated one on-premises deployment path absent a binding supported-horizon commitment.

The board approves selective repatriation as a governed stage rather than as an architecture, with gated review, named owners, a funded competitive selection returning at month eighteen, and verification by a party the audit committee engages rather than management.

title: From Collecting to Market Evidence: A Luigi Pikachu 296/XY-P Case Study on Grading, Comparability, and Decision Support

detail.abstract: This study asks whether the market value of the Luigi Pikachu 296/XY-P promotional card can be interpreted more clearly when only comparable evidence is used, and whether that process can support a practical grading decision tool. The dataset was built from completed sales, then cleaned by removing listings that did not match the exact card or transaction type. Currency context and evidence quality were kept visible instead of being compressed into a single market average. H1 received partial support, H2 could not be evaluated reliably because raw-card evidence was too limited, and H3 received the strongest support because stricter filtering reduced distortion from non-comparable listings. These findings shaped a calculator that organizes assumptions, grading costs, probability estimates, and uncertainty rather than promising a guaranteed return. A pilot study involving 14 external testers provided early evidence about whether the interface and recommendations were understandable. However, the project remains limited by thin raw-card coverage, the dominance of PSA-graded evidence, sensitivity to outliers, and the small convenience sample used for testing. Overall, the project supports a more transparent decision-making process while leaving broader market validation for future research.

title: The Covert Lever: How the Artificial Intelligence Subsidy Is Being Withdrawn, and Who Absorbs It

detail.title: The Covert Lever: How the Artificial Intelligence Subsidy Is Being Withdrawn, and Who Absorbs It

keywords: Quantity Reduction Against an Undisclosed Baseline

detail.abstract: Switching costs, consumer inattention, and shrinkflation together predict how a seller will pass a cost increase to a locked in buyer: by reducing the quantity supplied rather than raising the posted price, because consumers are measurably less sensitive to the first. This paper applies that prediction to the withdrawal of the flat rate subsidy in artificial intelligence services across 2025 and 2026, and reports three findings the packaged goods literature does not contain. First, a limiting case. A downsized grocery item still declares its quantity on the label, which is what makes downsizing measurable and what allows a price index to be corrected for it. Notion's usage allowance, live 3 August 2026, presents consumption as a percentage of a magnitude the company does not publish and reserves the right to change; Perplexity converted stated daily search allowances into unstated weekly ones. Quantity reduction against an undisclosed baseline is not merely unnoticed, as shrinkflation is; it is undetectable in principle and no series exists to correct. Second, a third instrument with no packaged goods analogue, in which the posted price and the stated allowance both hold and the rate at which ordinary work consumes the allowance moves. Anthropic reverted the Claude Code prompt cache default from one hour to five minutes in early March 2026 with no changelog entry, a change reconstructed by a user parsing 119,866 of his own API calls and associated with a 20 to 32 percent rise in cache creation cost, which the company then publicly said should not increase costs. Third, and decisively, the covertness is a choice rather than a property of the good. In the same market and the same months, Windsurf published per plan message estimates and grandfathered existing subscribers' prices through a structural change, Z.ai publishes approximate prompt limits per window and a schedule of peak and off peak quota multipliers, and Alibaba Cloud publishes the range of model calls a query consumes. The technical objection that these quantities cannot be disclosed is answered by sellers who disclose them. The paper assembles a chronology across eight sellers, tests whether the legibility of a change predicts its reversal and finds legibility necessary for organized objection but not sufficient for reversal with GitHub's fully disclosed June 2026 credit transition as the counterexample, and closes on Kahn v. Anthropic, PBC, a proposed class action filed 14 June 2026 alleging that Claude Max usage limits are hard to determine and were changed without clear notice. Limitations, five falsifiable predictions, and three disclosure remedies are set out.

title: Shared Functional Memory as Digital Cognitive Infrastructure: Corrective-Source Structure and the Scaling-Fragility Boundary of Agentic Organizing
affiliations: and George Mason University

detail.title: Shared Functional Memory as Digital Cognitive Infrastructure: Corrective-Source Structure and the Scaling-Fragility Boundary of Agentic Organizing
detail.abstract: Organizations increasingly deploy portfolios of AI agents that plan, use tools, and coordinate recurring work. These portfolios often rely on shared functional memory: an executable stock of business objects, operating rules, cases, task states, and exception criteria that multiple agents can invoke. Existing research explains how shared information expands processing capacity and how agent memory improves retrieval and task performance, but it does not explain how the source structure of shared memory changes organizational scalability and fragility. We distinguish two architectural properties. Shared deployment breadth is the range of agents, task stages, and consequential decision nodes covered by the same functional memory. Corrective-source availability is the extent to which those nodes retain independent data, retrieval paths, decision rules, or validation channels that can detect or correct a shared-memory error. A dual-path theory shows that broader deployment of reliable and deployable memory compresses local governance by reducing repeated context provision, interface coordination, and routine judgment. The same breadth also creates common exposure. When corrective sources are scarce, common exposure becomes common-source joint error, generating organizational burdens through propagation, detection, diagnosis, containment, and recovery. These opposing paths define a scalingfragility boundary beyond which further sharing no longer increases, and may reduce, the agent portfolio an employee can govern sustainably. The primary contribution extends organizational information-processing theory by distinguishing distribution capacity from corrective capacity. Digital infrastructures with equivalent speed, reach, and accessibility can support different organizational scales because they differ in whether consequential actions retain independent SHARED FUNCTIONAL MEMORY AND AGENTIC ORGANIZING 2 correction. Secondary implications connect organizational memory to cross-agent action dependence and span of control to the governance of shared digital infrastructure.

title: From Disclosure to Interpretability: Evaluating Algorithmic Transparency in Platform Governance
affiliations: , University of Missouri at Kansas City and Independent

detail.title: From Disclosure to Interpretability: Evaluating Algorithmic Transparency in Platform Governance

declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was given, and managed through our university's IRB (Institutional Review Board) mechanism
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by the Internet Society Foundation

detail.abstract: Social media recommender systems increasingly function as infrastructures of attention, shaping what users encounter, what appears salient, and what remains outside their field of view. Transparency has therefore become a central platform governance response, yet prevailing approaches often emphasize disclosure rather than whether affected audiences can understand, evaluate, and act on what is disclosed. This paper distinguishes disclosure-centered transparency from interpretability-centered transparency, and argues that transparency should be evaluated through demonstrated user understanding and actionability. Two exploratory pilot studies provide preliminary support for this distinction. Across the studies, outcomes moved selectively rather than uniformly. Greater awareness of platform harms did not translate straightforwardly into stronger action-oriented preferences, while exposure to simulated feeds produced modest movement in noticing feed characteristics but little broader change in understanding, response, or sustained practice. Greater social media feed content variety likewise did not consistently improve interpretability-related outcomes. Although varied social media feeds may reduce repetition or broaden exposure, these benefits are not equivalent to understanding how content was selected or what meaningful actions users can take. We therefore propose three governance reforms: standardized, contextual recommender system explanations; user controls whose effects can be observed and verified; and independent, recurring audits of explanation accuracy, comprehension, accessibility, actionability, and persistence. Together, these reforms can help shift transparency from formal availability toward demonstrable performance and offer a practical basis for strengthening US and international platform governance frameworks.

title: Behavioural Drift Intelligence for Institutional and Regulatory Early Warning: A Criminological and Evidence-Gated Agentic Artificial Intelligence Reference Architecture for Emerging Economic Crime Typologies

detail.title: Behavioural Drift Intelligence for Institutional and Regulatory Early Warning: A Criminological and Evidence-Gated Agentic Artificial Intelligence Reference Architecture for Emerging Economic Crime Typologies

keywords: Behavioural Drift Intelligence; Economic Crime; Financial Crime; anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing (AML/CFT); Typology Early Warning; Regulatory Intelligence; Financial Intelligence Units; Crime Scripts; Computational Criminology; Agentic Artificial Intelligence; Regulatory Technology; Evidence Gating; Multi-Agent Systems; Preventive Intervention

detail.abstract:
Economic crime controls often become most precise only after criminal methods have matured into recognisable patterns, regulatory warnings, enforcement themes, or monitoring scenarios. Existing dynamic risk assessment and customer-profiling systems can identify deviations from expected behaviour, but they do not systematically convert fragmented behavioural change into early-warning intelligence about the formation, mutation, convergence, displacement, or stabilisation of economic crime typologies. This paper identifies that delay as the typology-lag problem.

The paper introduces Behavioural Drift Intelligence (BDI), a criminologically grounded, evidence-gated agentic artificial intelligence reference architecture for institutional and regulatory early warning. Its central technical artefact is the BDI Typology Discovery MESH—Multi-Agent Evidence Synthesis and Hypothesis Testing. The MESH is designed to preserve evidence provenance, detect multi-level behavioural drift, generate competing, source-grounded and falsifiable typology hypotheses, compare them with known typologies, test source independence and lawful alternatives, and retain immature hypotheses within Machine Hypothesis Memory.

Only hypotheses satisfying transparent evidential and review-readiness criteria are promoted as Review-Ready Typology Hypotheses. A human hypothesis-validation gate determines whether a hypothesis has met the threshold for intelligence use. A separate action-authorisation layer determines whether validated intelligence warrants further evidence collection, control review, intelligence sharing, supervisory attention, regulatory reporting, or no immediate response.

Using conceptual design science, structured literature synthesis, requirements traceability, and ex ante conceptual design assessment, the paper derives fifteen design requirements and nine testable propositions. It also develops a behavioural drift taxonomy, typology status and novelty classification, Review-Ready Typology Hypothesis template, and Sectoral BDI Fusion Layer. The study does not implement or empirically validate BDI, claim quantified predictive performance, analyse proprietary customer-level data, or propose automated customer-level suspicion decisions.

BDI’s intended public value is to help financial institutions, financial intelligence units, and regulators recognise changing economic crime methods earlier, enabling faster intelligence sharing, control adaptation, supervisory attention, and proportionate preventive intervention before harm scales.

title: No Exchange Rate: Carbon in the Economics of AI Compute

detail.title: No Exchange Rate: Carbon in the Economics of AI Compute
detail.abstract: The emerging discipline of AI unit economics has identified a foundational measurement question: should computational efficiency be governed by intelligence per watt or by total cost of ownership per intelligence? This paper argues that the question identifies not a choice between competing metrics but the need for a broader measurement architecture. Financial cost, energy demand, and greenhouse gas emissions are distinct but interacting dimensions of AI production. Energy is monetized through electricity and infrastructure prices, while emissions depend on the timing, location, and supply conditions of consumption, and converting them into dollars requires a carbon value whose meaning varies across compliance systems, voluntary claims, policy appraisal, internal planning, and abatement decisions. No single value is suitable as a universal conversion factor, and a monetization is well formed only when its value, its emissions basis, and its decision purpose are mutually compatible. The appropriate architecture is a vector of financial, energy, and emissions measures, each normalized to a defined outcome, with contractual instruments registered beside the physical accounts rather than netted into them, reported figures derived from both under named rules, and with the decision rule made explicit through constraints, Pareto analysis, or shadow prices specific to a scenario. Proposed changes to electricity emissions accounting illustrate why the separation matters operationally: identical computational work can carry different financial, physical, and contractual attributes depending on when and where it runs. The result offers an extension to the emerging Tokenomics framework: the field's intelligence per watt and TCO per intelligence are both necessary, neither is sufficient, and the discipline's next task is to standardize how they operate alongside carbon.

title: Challenging Language Ambiguity: A Generative Approach to Automatic Data Labeling in Organization Research
affiliations: Tecnológico de Monterrey and Tecnológico de Monterrey

detail.title: Challenging Language Ambiguity: A Generative Approach to Automatic Data Labeling in Organization Research
detail.abstract: The proliferation of unstructured data in organizational contexts presents both an opportunity and a challenge: such information offers rich insights, but its analytical potential remains constrained by the need for human-labeled inputs. While human annotation is valuable, it often becomes imprecise, time-consuming, and difficult to scale. In response, generative AI (Gen AI) can serve as a credible and scalable alternative in contexts marked by semantic ambiguity and interpretive complexity. Leveraging information theory, we introduce an evaluative framework to assess whether Gen AI genuinely engages with textual ambiguity or merely reproduces surface patterns. Through comparative analysis across four datasets, two novel corpora and two public benchmarks, we find that Gen AI matches or exceeds human performance in ambiguous labeling contexts. Notably, few-shot prompting enhances alignment with human reasoning, suggesting that framing acts as a conceptual lever. These findings position Gen AI not merely as an automation tool, but as an interpretive collaborator, opening new paths for hybrid labeling pipelines in organizational research.

title: Harnessing the Wisdom of LLM Crowds Through Complementarity-Driven Iterative Collaboration
affiliations: , Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Antai College of Economics and Management and University of Connecticut - Department of Operations & Information Management

detail.title: Harnessing the Wisdom of LLM Crowds Through Complementarity-Driven Iterative Collaboration
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in enterprise contexts to support complex problem-solving tasks. Yet individual LLMs remain bounded by model-specific capability limitations. These heterogeneous capability boundaries pose a deployment challenge, but they also create an opportunity: strategically coordinating multiple LLMs may unlock collective intelligence that exceeds the performance of any single model. Existing approaches fix how models are combined in advance, overlooking the dynamic and state-dependent role of complementarity in complex LLM problem solving. Drawing on the wisdom-of-crowds paradigm, we reconceptualize collective LLM intelligence as relay-style complementarity: a sequential coordination process in which each successor model is selected to address the specific bottleneck identified in its predecessor's output. To operationalize this relay-style complementarity, we propose WILC (Wisdom Integration of LLM Crowds), a framework grounded in two design principles. First, iterative reflectionand-refinement establishes a state-preserving workflow through which models diagnose and refine prior outputs. Second, complementarity-driven model selection governs model transitions through a dual-gate mechanism: prospective complementarity fit (PCF) identifies the worker most suited to the current bottleneck, while posterior complementarity gain (PCG) evaluates whether the selected transition improves the evolving solution. Together, these design principles support strategic model transitions that refine answers through capability complementarity. Extensive experiments across four diverse benchmarks show that WILC achieves superior performance compared to existing approaches, including single-model self-refinement, ensemble methods, and dedicated query-routing methods. Under standardized pricing assumptions, WILC achieves comparable average benchmark performance to GPT-5.2 at approximately 7× lower estimated per-query cost, while facilitating data sovereignty through self-hosted deployment. This study contributes to IS research by extending wisdom-of-crowds theory from static aggregation to sequential AI complementarity and by providing transferable design principles for multi-AI coordination.

title: Seeing Through the ETF: Indicative NAV and Commodity Volatility Transmission
affiliations: Université Laval - Faculté d'Administration, Université Laval - Département de Finance et Assurance and Université Laval - Faculté d'Administration

detail.title: Seeing Through the ETF: Indicative NAV and Commodity Volatility Transmission
detail.abstract: This paper builds a novel dataset of indicative Net Asset Value (iNAV) observations for commodity ETFs and measures volatility transmission between ETFs and their underlying baskets using high-frequency realized variance. Applying this design to crude oil, gold, silver, and natural gas, we show that the iNAV provides a sharper image of the volatility relationship. Decomposing realized variance into continuous and jump components, we establish that transmission runs primarily through jumps rather than diffusion, a channel that standard volatility connectedness measures may obscure. Sampling frequency also matters: 1-minute data reveal daily volatility transmission up to twice as large as 30-minute estimates. Finally, transmission differs across commodity types. For gold and silver, it is unidirectional from iNAV to ETF, consistent with passive arbitrage. For energy ETFs, which are more liquid and hold futures as underlying assets, transmission is bidirectional and asymmetric.

title: When the Machine Writes the Ad: How Consumers Evaluate AI-Generated Advertising

detail.title: When the Machine Writes the Ad: How Consumers Evaluate AI-Generated Advertising

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: Generative AI tools now produce advertising content at scale, yet little is known about how consumers evaluate advertising when they become aware of its nonhuman origin. Existing theories of persuasion knowledge, source credibility, and perceived effort were developed for human persuasion agents and do not account for the evaluative challenges posed by a nonhuman source. This paper addresses that gap by proposing a conceptual framework centered on two contributions: (1) the evaluative disruption-recalibration process, which describes how consumers' established evaluative frameworks fail when applied to AI agents and are subsequently recalibrated along new dimensions; and (2) agent-nature uncertainty, a construct capturing the psychological state in which consumers find that their criteria for assessing persuasion agents are inadequate for a nonhuman entity. The framework identifies two dimensions of recalibration (agent recalibration and production recalibration), a disclosure-independent effort pathway, four moderating conditions, and derives eleven propositions and one research question. Implications for brand management and advertising governance under the EU AI Act are discussed. The paper argues that AI-generated advertising does not simply weaken existing evaluative processes but transforms them, producing a qualitatively different consumer response.

title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Consumer Behaviour, Purchase Intention, and Customer Satisfaction in the Digital Marketplace

detail.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Consumer Behaviour, Purchase Intention, and Customer Satisfaction in the Digital Marketplace
detail.abstract: The rapid rise of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies across digital commerce platforms has significantly transformed the landscape of consumer behaviour, reshaping the way consumers search for information, compare alternatives, and make purchasing decisions. This study investigates the multidimensional impact of AI on consumer behaviour, focusing on the role of AI-powered recommendation systems, personalized marketing, chatbots and virtual assistants, consumer trust, privacy concerns, purchase intention, and overall customer satisfaction. While a growing number of studies recognize the transformative opportunities of AI in marketing and commerce, major gaps remain regarding the integrated impact of these dimensions on consumer decision-making, particularly in emerging and developing markets, and regarding how individual differences such as digital literacy, age, and cultural orientation shape AI adoption. The proposed research follows a positivist, quantitative approach using a cross-sectional survey design (with an optional two-wave follow-up), employing a structured questionnaire based on established constructs from the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the Information Systems Success Model (ISSM), and Privacy Calculus Theory (PCT), supplemented by insights from Hofstede's cultural dimensions and behavioral-economics dual-process theory. The study will recruit a stratified random sample of 385 digital consumers from urban and semi-urban centres in India through online survey platforms, with quotas set by gender, age cohort, education, and city tier. Reliability and validity will be assessed via Cronbach's Alpha, Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA), and Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) using SPSS 27.0 and SmartPLS 4.0. Expected results indicate that AI-enabled recommendation systems and personalization significantly improve consumers' purchase intention, with consumer trust serving as an important mediating variable between AI interactions and purchase behaviour. Privacy concerns are expected to significantly and negatively moderate the relationship between AI personalization and purchase intention. Digital literacy, age cohort, and cultural orientation are expected to further moderate these relationships. The study contributes an integrated AI-Consumer Behaviour Model (AICBM) and offers practical managerial implications for marketers, AI developers, policymakers, and e-commerce platform operators seeking to deploy AI ethically and effectively. Limitations and future research directions are discussed.

title: Accidental Landlords: Behavioral Lock-In and Rental Market Spillovers

detail.title: Accidental Landlords: Behavioral Lock-In and Rental Market Spillovers
detail.abstract: Loss-averse homeowners facing nominal losses are reluctant to sell. A failed sale, however, need not keep them in place: they can list the property for rent and move, becoming “accidental landlords.” Using property-level data linking sale listings, rental listings, and transaction records in the U.K., I show that paper losses relative to the original purchase price strongly predict failed-sale-to-rent conversions. Rental conversion is sensitive to losses but not to gains, with the change in slope at the original purchase price. The channel operates through the failure of the attempted sale: paper losses reduce the probability of sale, while a roughly constant fraction of failed sales spills over into the rental market. Among properties that convert, owners facing paper losses set higher asking rents. At the aggregate level, regions with higher loss shares experience lower sales volume and more rental conversions. A one-standard-deviation increase in the loss share is associated with additional accidental-landlord entries equal to about 7% of total annual buy-to-let purchases. Reference dependence in the ownership market therefore affects how the housing stock is allocated between the ownership and rental markets.

title: From Dot-Com to AI: Technology Rebranding Twenty-Five Years Later
affiliations: University of Utah - David Eccles School of Business, University of Utah - David Eccles School of Business and University of Utah - David Eccles School of Business

detail.title: From Dot-Com to AI: Technology Rebranding Twenty-Five Years Later

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Michael J. Cooper has no relevant financial or non-financial interests to disclose. Hanjun Kim has no relevant financial or non-financial interests to disclose. Peter Y. Won has no relevant financial or non-financial interests to disclose.

detail.abstract: Twenty-five years ago, dot-com investors rewarded technology branding regardless of whether firms possessed the underlying technology. We examine 35 U.S. firms that changed their name, ticker, or both to emphasize artificial intelligence (AI) between 2020 and 2026. Unlike then, investors distinguish substantive AI activity from cosmetic AI rebranding: substantive rebranders earn cumulative abnormal returns 90 percentage points higher from one month before to three months after the rebranding. The advantage proves temporary, as both substantive and cosmetic AI rebranders subsequently experience sharp long-run reversals, suggesting that investors recognize genuine technological innovation but initially value it with excessive optimism.

title: Inflation and the Road to Socialism
affiliations: Pace University - Lubin School of Business

detail.title: Inflation and the Road to Socialism
detail.abstract: Since the end of World War II, U.S. monetary policy has been inflationary in character and intent. The dual mandate of the Federal Reserve (Fed) is to promote price stability and promote maximum employment. The Fed's definition of what constitutes price stability, however, is a matter of bureaucratic convenience. The Fed argues that moderate inflation is necessary to promote economic growth. The long-term and persistent erosion of the dollar's purchasing power, however, redistributes economic resources from the private to the public sector. This paper argues that this redistribution of economic power paves the way to socialism.

title: Axient: Empirical Calibration of Venue-agnostic Event-margin Protocols A Prospectively Frozen Analysis Plan, Deterministic Internal-alpha Technical Pilot, and Venue-emulator Methodology

detail.title: Axient: Empirical Calibration of Venue-agnostic Event-margin Protocols A Prospectively Frozen Analysis Plan, Deterministic Internal-alpha Technical Pilot, and Venue-emulator Methodology

detail.abstract:
The first two Axient studies establish a position-level debt-free-finality mechanism and a protocol-level on-chain credit and loss-allocation architecture for leveraged event markets. They do not establish that a live venue offers the execution depth, settlement reliability, close-window predictability, capital elasticity, or liquidation capacity required for deployment. This third study specifies the empirical bridge between mechanism design and a controlled private beta, and reports the first deterministic Internal Alpha technical pilot conducted under that framework.
     The prospectively frozen design separates book-implied, matched, settled, and redeemed value; scheduled and actual close; standalone and aggregate exit capacity; ordinary and adversarial liquidity response; Senior Credit LP and Liquidation Backstop Provider supply; market-maker commitment delivery; liquidation coverage; withdrawal dynamics; reserve use; and leverage eligibility for 2x, 3x, and 5x positions. Calibration and evaluation windows are separated, aggregate liquidity is measured on one shared execution curve, and no-go outcomes remain admissible conclusions. 
     The Internal Alpha evidence bundle contains twelve deterministic, synthetic, emulated-execution journeys. Ten journeys were admitted and completed; two were rejected before admission under registered risk or stale-data controls; all twelve were terminally classified. Valid root-event and complete-terminal-trace rates were 100 percent. Expected and observed state hashes matched across the exact Python model, Solidity contracts, services, and API projections. Unexplained reconciliation drift, duplicate-event financial delta, conflicting-evidence debt delta, external venue writes, and production asset movement were zero. Nineteen browser end-to-end tests, nineteen automated accessibility checks, three permission tests, and fifteen fault/recovery rehearsals passed. These results validate deterministic integration and evidence instrumentation for the registered synthetic paths only. 
     The pilot does not identify operational latency: every lifecycle timestamp is a synthetic scenario clock. title: Who Pays for Wildfires?

detail.title: Who Pays for Wildfires?
detail.abstract:
Sparks from private utility infrastructure have ignited some of the deadliest wildfires of the last decade. Climate change and a pattern of building in harm’s way have made the resulting harms catastrophic. Who should pay? This Article evaluates the liability and regulatory rules that answer that question, analyzing two categories of costs and their distributional implications: the damages wildfires impose (compensation) and the precautionary investments they require (infrastructure).

On compensation, the Article shows how the standard law-and-economics preference for strict liability is reversed in favor of negligence due to institutional features of the regulatory regime. Strict liability turns captive ratepayers into insurers for climate change, dulling incentives to address the housing and climate drivers of harm. The resulting electricity price increases undermine the clean energy transition by slowing the electrification – the adoption of electric vehicles, heat pumps, electric water heaters – decarbonization requires. The result is a perverse feedback loop: the legal response to wildfires worsens the climate conditions that make them destructive. And because ratepayers include renters while the beneficiaries are wealthier homeowners in high-risk areas, strict liability distributes burdens regressively.

On infrastructure, the Article argues for financing precaution through state taxpayers rather than ratepayers. Wildfire safety is a public good. Yet, the status quo effectively funds it through a commodity tax on electricity. This implied tax distorts consumption in favor of fossil fuels. It is also regressive, because it falls hardest on lower-income households. Financing wildfire safety through general state revenues would mitigate both these shortcomings.

The Article provides an analytical framework for evaluating the legal reforms that states are actively debating, and demonstrates how the reforms now gaining momentum, which shield utility shareholders and lean harder on ratepayers, point the wrong way.

title: How War Distorts International Trade: Gravity-Model Evidence from Europe after the Russia-Ukraine Conflict

detail.title: How War Distorts International Trade: Gravity-Model Evidence from Europe after the Russia-Ukraine Conflict
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how geopolitical conflict reshapes trade patterns, focusing on the economic consequences of the Russo-Ukrainian war on European and global trade flows. War is conceptualized as a shock that increases bilateral trade costs within a structural gravity model, rather than as a force acting against trade flows, amplifying frictions in territories closer to the epicenter and reducing the economic attractiveness of major trade routes. The empirical analysis combines an Extended Gravity Model based on bilateral trade data from 2019 and 2023 with geographic, institutional, and political factors, including sanctions regimes and energy specialization. The findings show that war not only reduces trade volumes but also operates multiplicatively on trade frictions, influencing both the intensity and direction of trade disruptions, with more pronounced effects in the central corridors of the European market. As a result, some trade relationships collapse while others are redirected towards less exposed regions; furthermore, policy choices are decisive in shaping trade flows and contribute to isolating the Russian economy by creating a policy-induced trade void around the target country, while mechanisms such as the EU Single Market facilitate the internal reallocation of trade flows, preserving economic cohesion.

title: Does the Dismissal of a Central Bank Governor Abroad Affect Monetary Policy at Home?
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and Swiss National Bank

detail.title: Does the Dismissal of a Central Bank Governor Abroad Affect Monetary Policy at Home?
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether the dismissal of a central bank governor (CBG) abroad spills over into domestic monetary policy. Using a novel dataset of 158 central banks (1987-2020), we estimate country-specific Taylor rules for 84 nations and apply the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem to identify policy deviations following foreign dismissals. We find that premature dismissals of foreign CBGs drive domestic policy rates below their Taylor-rule benchmarks under three conditions: (i) the foreign dismissal is preelectoral, (ii) the domestic country is a presidential democracy, and (iii) a domestic election is approaching. This accommodative compliance-where CBGs preemptively cut rates to mitigate their own dismissal risk-persists over a BIC-selected window of several months. Paradoxically, these rate cuts are more pronounced in countries with higher de jure independence. Hazard analysis confirms a dismissal contagion effect, showing that shorter-tenured domestic CBGs face a higher risk of termination following foreign dismissals.

detail.abstract: Nearly half of children exit foster care to adoption (non-relative or relative), guardianship, or living with other relatives (LWOR) arrangements. Yet, limited research has compared the longterm stability of these permanency types. We examine foster care exit cohorts 2008-2021 from the Adoption and Foster Care Analysis and Reporting System (AFCARS) from 12 states where pre-and post-adoption data linkage is possible. Outcomes examined were a maltreatment report within two years and reentry within three years of permanency exit. Controlling for child-level foster care experiences and demographics, results show that the odds of a maltreatment report were at least four times higher, and the odds of foster care reentry were at least six times higher, for LWOR and guardianship compared with non-relative adoptions. This pattern was observed in all 12 states and exit year cohorts. Differences between non-relative and relative adoption were small and varied by state and exit cohort.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the normative limits of libertarian paternalism in digital environments structured by algorithmic choice architectures. Libertarian paternalism generally assumes that freedom is preserved so long as individuals retain the formal possibility of choosing otherwise. In algorithmic environments, however, this assumption becomes insufficient. Recommendation systems do not merely present options; they filter, rank, and personalize the field of alternatives, often in ways that remain opaque to the agent. The paper therefore argues that the central issue is not whether choices are influenced, but whether agents can still recognize themselves reflectively in the choices they make. Drawing on Hegel's conception of freedom, it distinguishes between mediations that contribute to the formation of the will and forms of influence that merely administer behavior. Algorithmic systems may reduce complexity and support decision-making, but they may also narrow the horizon of meaningful alternatives and reinforce behavioral patterns that escape reflective appropriation. From this perspective, freedom cannot be reduced to the formal availability of options. It depends on whether the conditions of reflective self-recognition are preserved within the structures that shape choice.

Venue integrations are commonly tested through endpoint mocks, isolated order-lifecycle fixtures, or final-balance assertions. Those artifacts omit the ordered evidence needed to reproduce how a venue moved from market data to order acceptance, matching, settlement, close, or operational failure. The omission is material for event markets, where scheduled and actual close may differ, settlement can lag matching, and liquidity or connectivity can disappear precisely when a downstream system needs to reduce risk. 

     This paper specifies the Axient Venue Emulator Trace Dataset (AVET), a deterministic, provenance-aware publication format for event-venue emulator traces, and reports the canonical AVET v0.2.0 corpus. An AVET trace is a self-contained ordered event stream with source provenance, logical and observed clocks, causation identifiers, typed payloads, publication boundaries, and layered cryptographic identities. The specification distinguishes synthetic, rights-cleared derived, raw-permitted, hash-only, and private-not-distributed source classes. Public release is fail closed: raw third-party data, user identifiers, credentials, production writes, and production asset movement are prohibited unless an explicit rights and privacy decision permits them.

All traces pass the strict offline Draft 2020-12 schema and semantic validator; twelve malformed controls are rejected; the release's normative mutation and parity tests pass; and 98 manifest entries verify. Additional publication analysis detects 240 of 240 complete-trace identity mutations and obtains exact Python and Node.js agreement on 12,000 recursive key-order checks. detail.title: Climate Finance and the Green Economy: Carbon Pricing, Green Bonds, and Renewable Energy Subsidies A Review of the Economic Costs and Long-term Benefits of Climate Action
detail.abstract: Climate finance has moved from the margins of macroeconomic policy to its centre, as governments and capital markets search for instruments that can simultaneously curb greenhouse gas emissions and sustain growth. This paper presents a structured review of the economic literature on three pillars of the green economy — carbon pricing, green bonds, and renewable energy subsidies — and situates them within the broader question of whether the cost of climate action is justified by its long-term economic benefit. Drawing on more than fifty peer-reviewed studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and institutional reports published between 2006 and 2026, the review finds convergent evidence that carbon-pricing instruments have delivered statistically significant emission reductions without detectable harm to competitiveness, that green bonds carry a small but persistent yield discount (the "greenium") without additional credit risk, and that renewable-energy subsidies raise investment efficiency and employment even as their fiscal and distributional costs remain contested. On the cost-benefit question, the literature is unusually convergent for economics: mitigation investment in the range of roughly one to two percent of global GDP is consistently found to be far smaller than the five to twenty-percent-plus of GDP in damages projected under high-emission scenarios by mid-century. The review synthesises this evidence into policy implications for aligning carbon pricing, green-bond markets, and subsidy design, and identifies persistent gaps — particularly the shortfall between adaptation-finance needs and flows in developing economies — as priorities for future research.

detail.abstract: Digital technologies are reshaping global agri-food systems, redefining the relationship between farm production, market access, and rural household income. This review examines the contribution of three flagship digital interventions in Indian agriculture — the Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi (PM-KISAN) direct benefit transfer scheme, the electronic National Agriculture Market (e-NAM), and drone-based precision agriculture under the Namo Drone Didi and Kisan Drone initiatives — to farmer income and agricultural marketing efficiency, and reads the Indian experience through the lens of established economic theory: information economics (Stigler, 1961), transaction cost economics (Williamson, 1981), and the empirical literature on information and communication technology (ICT) in agricultural markets (Jensen, 2007; Aker, 2010; Goyal, 2010). Comparative evidence is drawn from China's rural e-commerce (“Taobao village”) movement, mobile-money-enabled agricultural finance in Sub-Saharan Africa (M-Pesa, Kenya), and the precision-farming provisions of the European Union's Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) 2023–2027. The review finds that PM-KISAN has measurably eased liquidity constraints and raised input investment among smallholders, though exclusion errors rooted in India's digital verification architecture persist; that e-NAM has improved price discovery within individual mandis but has not, on the best available econometric evidence, produced an economy-wide improvement in cross-market price integration, a shortfall better explained by transport infrastructure and unresolved state-level legal fragmentation than by any deficiency of the platform itself; and that drone technology shows real input-efficiency promise, best realised through collectively owned, fee-for-service delivery models that address the substantial capital-to-income affordability gap facing individual smallholders. Read together with the international comparison, the evidence suggests that digital delivery infrastructure (transfers, mobile money) generates more reliable income effects than digital marketplace re-engineering, and that institutional design — who owns the technology and on what terms — shapes inclusiveness as much as the technology itself. The paper closes with policy lessons of relevance well beyond India's borders.

detail.abstract: This paper maps the ownership, allocation and transaction pathways of global equity capital through the second quarter of 2026. It distinguishes institutional investors, pension and sovereign funds, mutual funds and exchange-traded funds, private equity and venture capital, family offices, retail investors, high-net-worth individuals and ultra-high-net-worth individuals. For each group, the analysis separates assets from current flows, investor domicile from target geography, and public equities from private transactions, IPOs and mergers and acquisitions. detail.title: Green Productivity and Economic Resilience: Evidence from Chinese Cities
detail.abstract: Does green productivity strengthen economic resilience, or can the adjustment costs associated with cleaner production make local economies more fragile? We examine this question using an annual panel of Chinese prefecture-level cities. We measure green productivity using green total factor productivity (GTFP) and economic resilience using a multidimensional index of resistance, recovery, adaptation, and renewal. Cities with higher green productivity exhibit greater economic resilience, and this relationship is robust to alternative samples, estimators, and resilience measures. The relationship becomes stronger when cities face earthquake damage, green-credit reallocation, or trade disruptions. The common pattern across shocks to physical capital, financing, and external demand is consistent with green productivity serving as a production-side buffer under stress. Climate-policy uncertainty, social financing, and digital financial development further condition this relationship. The findings identify both when the resilience value of green productivity becomes visible and which policy and financial environments help cities convert productive efficiency and flexibility into resilience.

detail.abstract: In December 2022, the Reserve Bank of India launched a retail pilot for the e-Rupee (e₹), India's central bank digital currency (CBDC), into an economy already served by the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), one of the world's largest and most successful digital payment systems. This review examines what three and a half years of retail e₹ operation reveal about central bank digital currency adoption in a market where a fast, free, and nearly universal digital payment rail already exists, and what the experience implies for the broader macroeconomic case for CBDC. Reading the evidence through the monetary economics of digital currency design — principally Kumhof and Noone's (2021) design-principles framework for containing bank disintermediation, and the wider literature on CBDC and monetary policy transmission — the review finds that India's retail e₹ had reached only 12 million cumulative users and roughly 175 million transactions by July 2026, against UPI's more than 400 million users and over 21 billion transactions processed in a single recent month. This gap is not unique to India: China's e-CNY, the world's largest live CBDC experiment by transaction value, had processed a cumulative ¥16.7 trillion by late 2025, a figure still smaller than the ¥279 trillion UnionPay's existing card network processed in 2025 alone. The review argues that this pattern is not an implementation failure so much as a predictable consequence of CBDC design choices — wallet holding caps, minimal or zero remuneration, and deliberately limited programmability — that were adopted precisely to contain the disintermediation risk the theoretical literature identifies, at the direct cost of the retail convenience needed to compete with an already-dominant incumbent payment rail. Where retail e₹ use has grown fastest, in India's programmable welfare-transfer pilots and in targeted currency-management applications, the underlying value proposition is different from, and complementary to, rather than competitive with, everyday retail payments. The review closes with a comparative reading of the European Central Bank's more cautious digital euro design and draws policy lessons for central banks weighing CBDC issuance into markets already served by effective private or public digital payment infrastructure.

detail.abstract: Geographical Indications (GIs) represent a vital form of intellectual property that links the quality and reputation of goods to their geographical origin. Bangladesh enacted the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 2013 to safeguard traditional products such as Jamdani sarees, Tangail sarees, and Rajshahi silk, while also fulfilling its obligations under the TRIPS Agreement. Despite the enactment of a dedicated legal framework, the practical implementation of GI protection in Bangladesh remains limited, with only a small number of products registered over more than a decade. The study argues that effective implementation of GI protection can significantly contribute to rural development, preservation of cultural heritage, and export-led economic growth in Bangladesh.

detail.abstract: Micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) are increasingly asked to produce financial and sustainability information for tax administrations, lenders, investors and value-chain partners, yet the reporting instruments they face were not designed for enterprises whose accounting capability is still forming. Building on a recent visibility-capability account of digitally mediated formalisation, under which digital infrastructures can make enterprises visible to institutions faster than they become able to respond, this paper asks how the existing stock of reporting instrumentslegislation, standards and intergovernmental guidance-should be sequenced and connected so that reporting capability can grow, proportionately and durably, towards integrated reporting. A structured integrative review-the evidence stage of a design-science architecture-combines empirical mechanism evidence, reporting and standard-setting sources, and administrative implementation evidence, validated on Scopus and Web of Science. The synthesis distinguishes four formalisation outcomes (entry, compliance deepening, taxable-revenue emergence and durability), four technology functions (transaction capture, enterprise accounting, analytical use and verification), and derives accordingly three design requirements: asynchronous progression of financial and sustainability reporting; the preparation of a basic (and comprehensive for more sophisticated communication needs) sustainability reporting document named 'Foundational Sustainability Data Schedule', shaped in accordance with both the EU voluntary standard on sustainability reporting and UNCTAD's Guidance on Core Indicators connected at each step to the financial reporting of the same stage; and measurement connectivity between material sustainability information and financial-statement estimates. The path is presented as a testable institutional architecture whose horizon-not whose claim-is integrated reporting.

title: Digital Death: Rethinking Smartphone Access in U.S. Prisons Through a Modern Reintegration and Behavioral Incentive Lens

detail.title: Digital Death: Rethinking Smartphone Access in U.S. Prisons Through a Modern Reintegration and Behavioral Incentive Lens
detail.abstract: United States corrections policy has long maintained a near-total ban on internet and smartphone access for incarcerated individuals. Historically justified under the rubric of institutional security, this policy of complete digital isolation now conflicts with the realities of a society in which essential functions, including employment applications, housing procurement, education, banking, and government benefits, are conducted almost exclusively online. This Article examines the systemic consequences of digital death: the total erasure of digital identity and literacy during incarceration. It surveys evolving international norms, comparative corrections practices in Scandinavia, Canada, and India, and empirical evidence demonstrating the link between digital connection, family contact, and reduced recidivism. This Article advances a specific and novel policy proposal: a behavioral incentive architecture that uses smartphone access as the primary lever for institutional conduct management. Under the proposed framework, access is not a blanket privilege but a calibrated behavioral reward, earned and maintained through compliance, program participation, and employment. The smartphone, equipped with Mobile Device Management controls, becomes simultaneously the institution's most powerful behavioral management tool and the incarcerated individual's primary preparation for reintegration into a digitized world. The Article also documents the impact of digital death on the 2.7 million children of incarcerated parents in the United States, argues that civil liberties organizations and corrections administrators share common ground on supervised access, examines the economics of replacing the current proprietary communication monopoly with an MDM-managed framework, and demonstrates that supervised legal access is the most effective tool available for reducing the contraband phone market. A full implementation roadmap, from Psychology Services endorsement through camp pilot to bureau-wide adoption, is provided.

title: Do Institutional Indices Measure Institutions? Evidence from the Worldwide Governance Indicators

detail.title: Do Institutional Indices Measure Institutions? Evidence from the Worldwide Governance Indicators
detail.abstract: Do widely used governance indicators measure institutions, or do they simply measure governance in general? This paper revisits a central assumption underlying empirical research in New Institutional Economics by examining whether the six components of the Worldwide Governance Indicators (WGI) capture two theoretically distinct concepts, institutional constraints and state capacity, or a single underlying governance dimension. Using panel data for 60 countries from 2004 to 2019 and validating the WGI against the Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) political corruption index, the results reveal a striking paradox. Although the six WGI components largely reflect a single underlying governance dimension, they differ markedly in how well they capture institutional constraints. Rule of Law, Voice and Accountability and Control of Corruption consistently align more closely with the independent corruption measure than Government Effectiveness, Regulatory Quality, and Political Stability. Moreover, a constraint-oriented index outperforms a capacity-oriented index, while the latter adds virtually no additional explanatory value. The findings question the common practice of treating all WGI components as interchangeable measures of institutional quality and call for greater attention to institutional measurement in comparative development research.

title: How Much Should We Trust the 30–40 Percent? Financial Knowledge and Retirement Wealth Inequality

detail.title: How Much Should We Trust the 30–40 Percent? Financial Knowledge and Retirement Wealth Inequality
detail.abstract: Financial knowledge reportedly explains 30–40 percent of retirement wealth inequality. We ask how much the flagship index explains. Reproducing the flagship model on its own code (21 of 21 moments), the attribution is not identified: the moments LMM match are compatible with knowledge shares of 16 percent under the assumed 4-point gradient and 1.5 percent under measured inputs. The data localize the gradient at 0.4 points, with a formal 95 percent interval [<0.2, 1.03]; 30–40 percent requires at least 1.81. Rebuilt with measured inputs, the model reproduces the wealth gap with knowledge shares under 3 percent.

title: Neighborhood Change and Local Economic Activity
affiliations: University of Rome Tor Vergata - Department of Economics and Finance and Rutgers University

detail.title: Neighborhood Change and Local Economic Activity
detail.abstract: We study how neighborhood change shapes local business demographics and employment. We use the regeneration of London public housing into mixed-income housing as a natural experiment that led to a large influx of more affluent households. In a difference-indifferences design comparing nearby businesses to those located farther away, we find that regenerations shift business composition-in both counts and employment-away from small local shops and toward larger general retail establishments and dining services that cater to the new residents. While we find no effect on total local employment on average, employment does increase in the areas most disadvantaged at baseline, suggesting that neighborhood change can expand local employment opportunities in these areas.

title: Swift's "A Modest Proposal" is an Economics Working Paper: A Reassessment of Swift (1729)

detail.title: Swift's "A Modest Proposal" is an Economics Working Paper: A Reassessment of Swift (1729)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract:
While Jonathan Swift's A Modest Proposal remains of interest, it has been reassessed by the standards of modern economics only once: Selwyn (1985) subjected the proposal to social cost-benefit analysis and found a high internal rate of return under the stated parameters. We continue the audit. This requires verifying the author's demographic and financial arithmetic, benchmarking his production parameters against modern reference data, and evaluating his welfare claims. Happily his three demographic subtractions each replicate exactly; less happily, his sole nontrivial division, the sex ratio of the breeding reserve, is given in two irreconcilable forms, and several of his parameters are extremely aggressive. For example, the birth weight he uses is above the 99.9th percentile of modern reference distributions, and the implied producer return of 400 percent per annum invites a supply response the author does not model. We replicate the author's static accounting but add a demographic stock-flow constraint omitted both by Swift and by the earlier reassessment. Our first result (Proposition 1) derives, under a deliberately favorable lower-bound model, a best-case replacement boundary in the mean inter-production interval, juvenile survival, and the length of the breeding career: depending on which of the author's two incompatible sex ratios one honors, his reserve of 20,000 can sustain an interval of no more than roughly 16 to 17 months, while his own quality parameter, a 28-pound terminal weight he couples with year-long nursing, implies a production interval of roughly two years under standard fertility accounting. Therefore the quantity and quality sides of his proposal cannot jointly hold; under the standard demographic benchmark the failure is sharper still, the advertised flow requiring a negative postpartum infecundable period and so failing even before nursing
is reckoned in (Proposition 2). Applying the same accounting to the larger stock the author’s
own reserve implies merely relocates the impossibility: at the upper empirical calibration,
the scheme would require between 112 and 119 percent of live-born units to survive to mar-
ket. Most significantly, we point out that general-equilibrium effects, principally the annual
withdrawal of 100,000 one-year-olds from the cohort that would otherwise enter the future
labor force, are unaddressed. We conclude that the proposal is infeasible on its own terms,
failing at once in its annual output and, a breeding cycle later, in the replacement of its
stock.

detail.abstract: Ethiopia has experienced one of the most significant monetary policy reforms in its recent economic history. For decades, monetary policy relied on direct instruments, including administrative credit controls, regulated interest rates, and central bank financing of government deficits. These policies constrained financial market development and weakened monetary policy transmission. In 2024, the National Bank of Ethiopia (NBE) initiated comprehensive monetary and financial sector reforms to establish an interest-rate-based monetary policy framework. A central component of these reforms was the modernization of the Treasury bill (T-bill) market. During the transition period, a temporary credit growth cap was introduced to contain inflation while the market-based framework was being developed. Following the removal of the credit cap in 2026, Treasury bills became the principal instrument for liquidity management and open market operations. This article reviews the evolution of Ethiopia's Treasury bill market across the pre-reform, transition, and post-transition periods and discusses its implications for monetary policy and financial market development.

title: Bayesian Conjugate Gradient for Fast Compute: Data Augmentation and Krylov Solvers for Modern LLM Training
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Bayesian Conjugate Gradient for Fast Compute: Data Augmentation and Krylov Solvers for Modern LLM Training
detail.abstract: We show that the dominant cost of training and fine-tuning modern language models is a sequence of ill-conditioned linear solves, and that a Bayesian treatment of those solves delivers both a fast algorithm and calibrated uncertainty at no additional order of cost. The construction has two ingredients. First, the data-augmentation theory of Polson and Scott [2013] and Polson et al. [2013] turns non-Gaussian likelihoods, including the logistic and softmax losses that define next-token prediction, into conditionally Gaussian models with precision matrix Q = T + V ⊤ ΩV. Second, conjugate gradient solves systems in Q using only matrix-vector products, which is exactly the primitive that accelerator hardware executes efficiently, and which for adapter and output-head parameterisations coincides with a forward and backward pass. We give a spectral analysis showing that the Jacobi-preconditioned augmented precision matrix has a bounded effective condition number after removal of K + 1 outlying eigenvalues, where K is the number of crossed factors in the design, so that the number of Krylov iterations is free of the parameter dimension. A perturbation-optimisation step converts the same solve into an exact draw from the conditional posterior, and the Bayesian conjugate gradient posterior of Cockayne et al. [2019] supplies an error model for the truncated solve. We prove that Polya-Gamma augmentation inflates the effective condition number by at most the square of the ratio of the largest to the smallest latent scale, a quantity that is logarithmic in sample size under bounded logits. Simulations on crossed designs with up to p ≈ 9 × 10 4 parameters show conjugate gradient cost growing close to linearly in the problem size while sparse Cholesky cost grows cubically, with iteration counts flat in dimension. On two real corpora, using skip-gram with negative sampling, the augmented precision has condition number 1.2 × 10 6 and effective condition number 1.35, and the solver converges in 23 iterations; the predicted K small eigenvalues and largest eigenvalue near K + 1 appear to three significant figures. Against an exact Cholesky sampler the truncated scheme agrees to 10-9 posterior standard deviations at tolerance 10-8 and fails sharply below 10-3. Against a tuned Adam baseline it needs 1.8 times fewer data passes to reach suboptimality 10-6 , though it is slower to one digit of accuracy. We also report a negative result: prior preconditioning, which is effective for sparse regression, degrades badly in the crossed-design regime relevant to embedding tables.

title: Family, Stigma, and Social Recognition After Addiction

detail.title: Family, Stigma, and Social Recognition After Addiction

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that she has no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
