detail.title: The Law of the Algorithmic State in Central and Eastern Europe
detail.abstract: The paper is an introduction to a special issue of the Italian Journal of Public Law on the law of the algorithmic state in Central and Eastern Europe. It explains why the issue focuses on the state as developer and user of emerging technologies, and on Central and Eastern European countries as the relevant units of comparison. The paper gives some further insights about the methodology adopted in making the issue and about the main comparative lessons learned from this collective endeavour.

title: The Most Important Human Skills for the Age of AI and the Future of Work: FILE — The Five Intelligences of Leadership Evolution

detail.title: The Most Important Human Skills for the Age of AI and the Future of Work: FILE — The Five Intelligences of Leadership Evolution

keywords: Leadership in The Age of AI

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence changes what organizations can do; human leadership must decide what should be done, what remains accountable, and what must never be surrendered to machines. This working paper presents FILE — the Five Intelligences of Leadership Evolution — as a human-centered management theory and diagnostic framework for responsible leadership and decision-making in the age of AI. FILE argues that the most important human skills for the AI era and the future of work require the integrated exercise of five meta-intelligences: Augmented Intelligence, Emotional Intelligence, Cultural Intelligence, Political Intelligence, and Adaptive Intelligence. The paper defines the FILE formula, maps the framework onto the human hand, presents the 70 nested intelligences of FILE, explains five emergent outcomes, and develops RC — The Relational Commons as the shared human ecosystem that leadership must protect, cultivate, and renew. It also clarifies boundaries among adjacent intelligences, offers a diagnostic application to AI-supported employee performance evaluation, and states limitations and future research directions. Its purpose is to establish a public, citable, and timestamped record of FILE as a management theory of human leadership in the age of AI.

title: Digital Vulnerability for All?
affiliations: University of Trieste and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Digital Vulnerability for All?

publicationDetails.detailsText: Camilla Crea and Marta Infantino (eds.), Remedies to Digital Vulnerability in European Private Law. Pathways towards Fairness, Springer, 2025, 335-360

detail.abstract: What if we took seriously the idea recently put forward by many institutions and scholars that, in online interactions, all human beings are vulnerable or made more vulnerable than ordinary? What if our regulatory infrastructures acknowledged that the vast majority of us, even in the hyperconnected societies of the Global North, have little understanding of the digital infrastructure on which we depend? This chapter aims to explore these questions and propose a new interpretive framework, using European private law as a testing ground at the crossroads of national and European Union rules. In particular, it investigates whether assuming that we are all vulnerable might reduce the protection for those who belong to protected categories and are at heightened risk of cumulative and intersectional discrimination. It tests whether embracing digital vulnerability as a universal condition would lead to an unacceptable level of personalization of the law and burden corporations and individuals with excessive vulnerability-related duties. The chapter also verifies whether and how vulnerability-related duties might be enforceable in the borderless digital environment. All of the above will hopefully help challenge current interpretive views that deny any relevance to online defenselessness.

title: Contract Design and Bus Electrification: Evidence from Santiago, Chile
affiliations: Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile

detail.title: Contract Design and Bus Electrification: Evidence from Santiago, Chile
detail.abstract: Santiago went from about 100 electric buses in 2018 to nearly 4,400 by early 2026, the largest electric-bus fleet outside China. This paper analyzes the contract design behind the transition. Successive tenders unbundled service operation from fleet ownership and charging infrastructure. They turned buses and terminals into concession-dedicated assets that transfer to the next operator. They also paid fleet financing through fixed monthly installments, administered centrally and owed regardless of which operator runs the route. This design removed the two risks that make lenders charge a premium on transit assets: stranding at contract end and operator default. It made electric capital financeable without operators bearing it. A permanent subsidy, created in 2009, made the long payment horizons credible. Competition widened accordingly: participation rose from 16 offers in 2019 to 84 in 2023, and the monthly fleet installment per electric bus fell by 10 to 25 percent. Using payment and tender records, I show that electrification did not materially change the cost per kilometer of service and did not require a new funding source. The 2019 bids priced both technologies under the same contracts. They imply that renewing the fleet with new diesel buses would not have been cheaper per kilometer. I conclude with policy lessons and the conditions under which the model transfers to other cities.

title: Unreasonable Assurance: The Auditing Industry Meets the DSA's Systemic Risk Regime
affiliations: University of Amsterdam - Institute for Information Law (IViR), University of Amsterdam - Institute for Information Law (IViR) and University of Amsterdam

detail.title: Unreasonable Assurance: The Auditing Industry Meets the DSA's Systemic Risk Regime

detail.abstract: The Digital Services Act introduces a regulatory obligation requiring very large online platforms and search engines to identify and mitigate systemic risks linked to their services, which, under Article 37, must undergo independent audits on a yearly basis. This emerging "audit ecosystem" places auditing firms in an uneasy position: while they are expected to deliver assessments of reasonable assurance, they themselves often frame their role as necessarily limited, procedural, and dependent on client-provided evidence. To address these tensions, this paper adopts an actor-centred perspective on the DSA's audit framework and based on an expert workshop with auditors and DSA researchers, provides insights on how the system is understood and enacted by those implementing it in practice. We present four (epistemic, methodological, professional and structural/political) core issues regarding auditors' role and expectations within the framework. Finally, this paper invites to reflect on the auditor role within the DSA enforcement, raising fundamental questions about who is and should be positioned to take auditing responsibilities in the realm of systemic risks, given its constructive ambiguity as an essentially contested and socially constructed concept, that reflects, rather than challenges existing power relations.

title: Pooled, Window, and Sequential Frontiers in Stochastic Frontier Analysis: Matched Parametric Counterparts to Panel DEA in a By-production Framework

detail.title: Pooled, Window, and Sequential Frontiers in Stochastic Frontier Analysis: Matched Parametric Counterparts to Panel DEA in a By-production Framework

detail.abstract: Nonparametric efficiency analysis chooses its benchmark technology through reference-set constructions — contemporaneous, pooled, window, and sequential frontiers — while stochastic frontier analysis (SFA) is silent about which observations define the frontier at each date, so applied DEA–SFA comparisons routinely pair mismatched frontier concepts. We develop the matched parametric counterparts. The sequential construction, which rules out technological regress by expanding the reference set through time, receives a genuinely new counterpart: expanding-sample SFA under a no-regress inequality restriction on technical change, implemented by constrained maximum likelihood and by Bayesian estimation with the restriction in the prior support, including recursive-prior and pointwise-dominance variants. Applied alongside matched DEA to a by-production system (electricity, SO2, NOx) for 92 U.S. coal-fired plants spanning the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments, three results are central. First, the constraint binds in nine or ten of ten vintages for the only specification detecting SO2 inefficiency — yet never significantly — so the boundary-inference problem afflicting constrained ML is pervasive and the Bayesian implementation earns its keep. Second, the apparent regress dissolves under richer error structures, most decisively under plant random effects, whose plant-conditional predictions dominate every pooled-error specification; the robust verdict is persistent, regulation-correlated heterogeneity rather than technical regress. Third, matched DEA–SFA agreement tracks the strength of the identified inefficiency signal: sequential SO2 rank correlations exceed 0.94, against 0.33 for the pooled intended-output comparison.

detail.abstract: California’s statewide menthol cigarette ban creates a central empirical puzzle: while legal sales of menthol cigarettes fall to near zero following the policy, menthol smoking persists. This study investigates the mechanisms underlying this divergence using retail scanner data, population-based surveys, and an original survey of California smokers. Retail data confirm that menthol cigarettes were effectively removed from the legal market, but the decline is accompanied by substitution toward non-menthol cigarettes and menthol-like products. At the same time, population-based surveys indicate no meaningful change in smoking prevalence and continued menthol use. To reconcile these patterns, we use original survey data with within-individual variation to examine behavioral responses directly. We find that 63 percent of menthol smokers continue to report menthol use after the ban, 21 percent switch to non-menthol cigarettes, and few quit. Hazard model estimates show no sustained increase in cessation. The findings indicate that the menthol ban primarily reshapes product composition rather than reducing smoking. Behavioral adjustment occurs mainly through substitution and continued access via existing illicit markets, highlighting the importance of accounting for consumer responses when evaluating product-based tobacco regulations.

title: A Third Anchor for Global Liquidity: Intellectual Capital Money as a Non-Sovereign Reserve Asset
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: A Third Anchor for Global Liquidity: Intellectual Capital Money as a Non-Sovereign Reserve Asset
detail.abstract: Global liquidity depends on three interlocking functions: elastic funding, credible reserve assets, and effective official backstops. In the present system, all three rest on the debt of a small number of sovereigns-in practice, largely one. This paper asks whether a productive, non-sovereign class of underlying assets could support reserve-asset creation without reproducing the logic of sovereign-debt expansion. Proposals for supranational reserve assets are not new. What they have consistently left unresolved is a prior question: what should determine the quantity of reserve assets issued? Only two answers have been available-political allocation, as with quota-based allocations of Special Drawing Rights, and the fiscal deficits of a single issuer. I propose a third: the realized volume of transactions in intellectual capital. I develop the institutional design of Intellectual Capital Money (IKM), a claim issued when a transaction in protected intellectual capital is financed, in an amount equal to the negotiated price of that transaction. The obligation constituting IKM is a treaty commitment, binding on all member states, to exchange IKM for member government securities on demand. IKM is therefore non-sovereign debt backed by a diversified pool of sovereign assets. Two implications follow. First, IKM accrues not to the economy in which the rights holder is located but to the economy in which the implementer is located. This implementer-side principle substantially limits the force of the concentration and procyclicality objections. Second, when reserve supply is tied to a productive base rather than to the accumulated liabilities of a single issuer, the sign of the feedback between supply and credibility may reverse. I calibrate this claim: the multiplier exceeds unity but is bounded, and five structural asymmetries make the downward multiplier smaller than the upward one. This is a working paper. Formalization of the sign reversal, the time consistency of the treaty obligation, and quantitative estimates of issuance are left to further work.

title: Measuring the Reliability of Backtest Validation
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Measuring the Reliability of Backtest Validation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.

detail.abstract: Before trusting a backtest, practitioners pass it through layers of statistical controls: a robust standard error, a multiple-testing correction, a cross-validation scheme. The working assumption is that each added control makes a validated strategy more trustworthy. We test this assumption by treating the whole validation protocol as a single estimator, whose realized size and power we measure by Monte Carlo simulation with planted ground truth. Protocols are compared only after calibration to the same size. A control improves reliability only when it covers a failure mode left open. Stacking two corrections against the same failure leaves the false-positive rate unchanged and destroys power, and redundancy is decided at the level of the failure sub-mode rather than the family, so two controls from the same family can still be complementary. We measure this across return regimes and resampling schemes, then read a third property that size and power cannot see: how often a protocol validates an edge that has already died. From these measurements we derive a composition rule and a small class of pipelines that satisfies it. At a realistic search scale, honest validation doubles the minimum detectable edge. The benchmark and the code library 1 behind every result are released. The paper proposes no new corrections, only a measurement of how the existing ones combine.

title: Does the Itô Correction Contain Independent Predictive Information? Evidence from Regime-Weighted Volatility Dynamics

detail.title: Does the Itô Correction Contain Independent Predictive Information? Evidence from Regime-Weighted Volatility Dynamics
detail.abstract: This paper constructs a dynamic, regime-weighted Ito correction signal from a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) applied to S&P 500 returns and tests its predictive content for future equity returns. The expected volatility drag-weighted by HMM filtered regime probabilities-contains independent predictive information beyond realised volatility and the VIX. Recursive out-of-sample (OOS) tests on 2016-2024 produce R 2 = 2.32%, compared to a benchmark OOS R 2 of-3.47%, confirming genuine predictive gain over the prevailing-mean model. Clark-West tests confirm statistically significant mean squared prediction error (MSPE) reduction (CW = 7.581, p < 0.001). detail.abstract: We analyse the 1994 devaluation of the CFA franc using a panel of 31 African countries (1961-2022), including 11 from the CFA zone, using a difference-indifferences approach with permutation inference. Consistent with rigorous re-evaluations in the recent literature, we find no robust effect on GDP per capita at any time horizon, up to 28 years after the shock. Seven heterogeneity tests fail to explain the zero effect on GDP. These findings warrant caution when considering the benefits of devaluations within monetary unions including primary commodity economies.

detail.abstract: This study examines whether corporate investments in artificial intelligence (AI) governance frameworks pay off in the consumer market by linking corporate disclosure styles with consumer valuations. In Stage 1, we conduct a computational text analysis using Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency vectorization and Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection dimension reduction on the inaugural transparency reports (N = 25) submitted to the Hiroshima AI Process. The results indicate that the communication posture of Japanese enterprises forms a distinct latent profile within this sample, prioritizing formalized organizational oversight and multi-stakeholder risk management over code-level optimization. In Stage 2, these disclosure styles are operationalized into a scenario-based statedpreference survey of Japanese consumers (N = 887) using the contingent valuation method. Selection-corrected estimates suggest that consumers value internal governance rules under routine conditions, but privacy-sensitive respondents discount unverified self-reporting. In higher-price settings, AI-literate respondents who initially prefer the technology-oriented provider demand substantially larger discounts for the governance-oriented alternative, while audited governance functions primarily as a selection prerequisite rather than a continuous willingness-to-pay premium. After a simulated operational failure, ex-ante organizational governance narratives are associated with lower customer attrition, acting as a provider-specific behavioral buffer. These findings clarify the potential and limitations of voluntary AI governance disclosure, providing an empirical basis for policy instruments designed to address information-driven market failures and strengthen co-regulatory safety architectures.

detail.abstract: Fractal geometry provides a rigorous framework for describing the irregularity, heterogeneity, and scale-dependent behavior of subsurface reservoir systems. Fractal concepts have been widely applied to characterize fracture networks, pore-throat structures, pressure-transient responses, anomalous diffusion, multiphase flow, digital-rock properties, and transport processes in complex porous media in oil, gas, and geothermal reservoirs. This review presents a structured and critical synthesis of fractal geometry and anomalous-diffusion approaches in reservoir engineering. Fundamental concepts, including fractal dimension, Euclidean dimension, network topology, random walks, and anomalous transport, are first introduced to establish the theoretical basis. Subsequently, key modeling frameworks-namely the Chang and Yortsos fractal reservoir model, the Metzler fractional-diffusion model, and the Raghavan anomalous-diffusion formulation-are critically discussed with respect to their physical assumptions, model parameters, and applicability. The paper then reviews applications across fracture-dominated geothermal systems, naturally fractured petroleum reservoirs, unconventional and hydraulically fractured reservoirs, pore-scale characterization, multiphase-flow modeling, digital-rock analysis, acidizing, wormhole growth, and production-related applications. Special attention is given to the distinction between geometric fractal parameters derived from images, pore-size distributions, or fracture maps and dynamic anomalous-transport parameters inferred from pressure, production, or tracer data. Finally, limitations related to parameter estimation, scale dependency, model uncertainty, and physical validation are evaluated, and future research directions are proposed, emphasizing integrated multiscale characterization, digital-rock physics, uncertainty quantification, field validation, hybrid data-driven workflows, and coupled multiphysics modeling.

title: Aegis Equity: A Falsification-Driven Framework for Quantitative Trading and Model Risk Management in Investment Banking

detail.title: Aegis Equity: A Falsification-Driven Framework for Quantitative Trading and Model Risk Management in Investment Banking
detail.abstract:
The proliferation of machine learning tools has made it straightforward to construct a quantitative trading strategy that generates impressive historical performance. The same tools have made it equally straightforward to construct a strategy that merely appears to perform well, one whose apparent edge is an artifact of overfitting, data leakage, or multiple testing rather than genuine predictive skill. Distinguishing between the two is the central methodological challenge of applied quantitative finance, and the primary contribution of this thesis.

This research constructs, validates, and deliberately attempts to falsify Aegis Equity, a dual LightGBM classifier trained on 14 endogenous price-and-volume features, applied to the NSE 500 universe with a Beta-Switch regime filter that dynamically allocates capital between stock-picking, index exposure, and defensive cash. The system is evaluated through a pre-registered three-gate falsification protocol in which all thresholds, hypotheses, and decision rules are locked before the out-of-sample window (January 2019 to October 2023) is examined.

Gate 1 confirms the machine learning models possess statistically significant trade-level predictive skill. Gate 2 formally rejects naive portfolio translation, demonstrating that trade-level skill alone is insufficient to generate portfolio-level outperformance during systemic market shocks. Gate 3 confirms that the Beta-Switch regime filter resolves this failure: the validated architecture achieves a Sharpe ratio of 2.2461 against a benchmark Sharpe of 0.7784, clearing a Bonferroni-corrected block bootstrap threshold of p < 0.0166 across all three tested block sizes.

The thesis documents five backtest construction failure modes, narrative inflation, feature-level data leakage, execution logic bugs, temporal scope violations, and statistical misalignment, each detected through artifact-level verification rather than statistical flagging, along with a sixth discarded test whose invalidity is documented rather than hidden. These findings are mapped onto the model governance practices of investment banking institutions, demonstrating that the three-gate protocol is a practical, working implementation of the independent validation principles mandated by regulatory frameworks including SR 11-7.

title: No Test, No Claim: Untested Code is Vibed Code Verification as the Price Signal of Correctness

detail.title: No Test, No Claim: Untested Code is Vibed Code Verification as the Price Signal of Correctness
detail.abstract:
When a large language model writes code we do not trust, we tend to blame the author: a machine wrote it, so it must be suspect. This paper argues that the instinct points at the wrong variable. What makes code trustworthy is not who wrote it but whether reproducible evidence exists that it does what it claims.

Authorship is inert; verification is everything. We defend one thesis - untested code is vibed code, whether a human or a model wrote it - and build it as a single argument rather than a tour of disciplines.

We begin where the argument is strongest: a correctness claim about untested code has no content. It is an unsigned promise (Design by Contract), an unfalsifiable assertion (Popper), and, in Alf Ross's sense, a tû-tû -- a bookkeeping word that connects a wish to a reliance while denoting nothing in between - because the theory that would give it content, in Naur's sense, never leaves the author's head.

Authorship cannot supply that content: a private, perishable understanding is, on Nozick's truth-tracking account, a belief that would persist even if the code were broken, which is to say not knowledge at all, and  the human author and the model collapse into the same case. A program's real
law is its behavior in execution - the legal realists' law in action - not the paper rules of its names, types, and comments; the test is the court decision that discloses it. What running on vibes costs is then contested ground: the cost splits cleanly into a part that can be priced and a part that
cannot.

Chicago prices the first (the Learned Hand formula renders a cheap omitted test negligent by construction; the market for lemons explains why
untested modules cannot be told from working ones); Austrian marks the limit of the second (the calculation problem; dispersed, tacit knowledge) -- and the test is what a decision-maker needs at exactly that boundary, the decentralized feedback signal that substitutes for a global correctness calculation no one can perform. We make the cost concrete with a compound-Poisson actuarial model, of which the Hand formula is the point-estimate special case, and an estimable panel specification, then bound its pretensions with the Austrian caveat that its parameters are guesses at a moving target. The practical contribution follows from that model. Because operational-risk capital under Basel II and Solvency II is itself a
compound-Poisson loss distribution, a test is an operational-risk control with a measurable effect on regulatory capital; the Learned Hand formula is the deterministic point estimate of that model's pure premium; and the industry's faith in "battle-tested" code systematically under-reserves the tail in which latent security failures -- Dirty COW, the XZ backdoor -- actually live, because production tenure samples the body of the loss distribution and never it's tail.

Under every step the same verdict returns, and none of them can find authorship on the relevant side of the ledger.

detail.title: Dynamic Income-Oriented Pension Investment Model
detail.abstract: We present a stochastic dynamic model of retirement saving with maximization of the expected utility of pension income. In contrast to traditional models, we change the paradigm from value-oriented to incomeoriented. The model uses SeLFIES (Standard-of-Living Forward-starting Income-only Securities) as risk-free assets. SeLFIES has a dened stream of payments starting at retirement for a dened period. Payments are indexed by consumption per capita or ination from the time of issuance. The paradigm change from value-oriented to income-oriented causes a change in the risk ranking of assets. Government bonds with longer maturities are less risky assets compared to those with shorter maturities. We present the optimal level of savings in the form of a certainty equivalent and an internal rate of return of the certainty equivalent. In addition, we calculate the time evolution of the optimal allocation of investments into dierent types of assets. Optimal saving strategies deliver satisfactory replacement rates.

detail.abstract: In this paper, we study the impact of a shock-dependent Phillips Curve on growth and exchange rate dynamics in six African countries from 1980 to 2024. In contrast to the standard Phillips Curve, this model permits the inflation-output trade-off to depend on the type of structural shocks, allowing for nonlinear and state-contingent relations in the macroeconomy. The novel empirical toolkit developed for this analysis utilizes Panel SVAR, Conditional Inverse Rosenblatt (CIR)-based impulse responses, and Panel Generalized Linear Models (GLM) to systematically explore short-and medium-term transmission mechanisms across diverse economies. The results exhibit considerable crosscountry heterogeneity. The shock-driven Phillips Curve has a statistically significant negative impact on growth in South Africa, Nigeria, Egypt, and Algeria, with the influence on Ethiopia and Uganda being weak/insignificant, an indication of structural rigidities and feeble monetary transmission. Exchange rate responses tend to be temporary and differ across regimes, being stronger in more open and financially integrated countries. Impulse response analysis shows that inflation shocks transitorily raise output and exchange rate volatility, but these effects vanish as predicted by the long-run neutrality. These results suggest that macroeconomic relationships in African countries are nonlinear, heterogeneous, and state-dependent, which have implications for the design of monetary policy and the conduct of macroeconomic stabilization.

title: Quantitative Credit Risk Modeling and Failure Analytics: A Historical Comparative Discriminant Case Study of Pakistan's Cement Sector

detail.title: Quantitative Credit Risk Modeling and Failure Analytics: A Historical Comparative Discriminant Case Study of Pakistan's Cement Sector
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the quantitative credit risk dynamics and corporate insolvency forecasting within Pakistan's heavy manufacturing domain through an empirical historical evaluation of the cement sector over the financial years 2017 to 2019. Capital-intensive industrial sectors in emerging economies face severe structural vulnerabilities driven by macroeconomic volatility, debt-servicing burdens, and cyclical revenue shocks. Utilizing Edward I. Altman's Five-Factor Multivariate Discriminant Analysis (MDA) Z-Score architecture, this study evaluates the solvency profiles, operational efficiencies, and leverage stability of five dominant listed cement manufacturers: Lucky Cement Limited, D.G. Khan Cement Company Limited, Kohat Cement Company Limited, Maple Leaf Cement Factory Limited, and Attock Cement (Pakistan) Limited. Empirical findings reveal a pronounced, systemic deterioration in financial stability across the three-year horizon. The sample's composite mean Z-score contracted sharply from a robust "Safe" baseline of 4.48 in FY2017 to a transitional "Grey" state of 2.86 in FY2018, ultimately plunging into the "Distress" threshold at 1.51 in FY2019. Working capital compression (X1) and collapsing equity-to-liability ratios (X4) served as the primary quantitative catalysts driving firm-level distress. This research advances financial engineering applications in corporate risk management by highlighting the diagnostic efficacy of multi-ratio linear discriminant algorithms for pre-emptive insolvency engineering in emerging markets.

detail.abstract: Cross-border mergers and acquisitions are a central route to scale, capability acquisition and market entry in Europe, yet their outcomes vary sharply. This paper develops an exploratory process-capability framework for analysing value creation in the European mid-market, where founder ownership, limited public information, thin management structures and institutional heterogeneity make execution especially consequential. The study combines an integrative review of the strategy, corporate finance and postmerger integration literature with descriptive secondary market evidence and a comparative analysis of three deliberately selected boundary cases: Amplifon-GAES, Lavazza-Carte Noire and Aryzta-Picard. The paper does not treat the cases as a representative sample. Instead, it uses them to elaborate six propositions concerning governance fit, origination advantage, the bankability of improvements, contingent deal structure, preservation-first integration and codified acquisition learning. The central argument is that acquirer value is not explained by strategic rationale alone. It depends on whether control rights match the intended value-creation mechanism; whether the buyer has an information or process advantage before signing; whether the price reflects only improvements that are sufficiently within the buyer's control; and whether integration protects the tacit and relational capabilities that justified the acquisition. The framework contributes a practical bridge between M&A process research and valuation discipline and identifies testable implications for corporate acquirers, private equity sponsors and advisers operating in fragmented European markets.

detail.abstract: This report compares the human development of three neighbouring Middle Eastern states, Iran (Islamic Republic of), Saudi Arabia and Türkiye, across the period 1990 to 2023, using a full annual data series drawn primarily from the United Nations Development Programme's Human Development Report 2025 and the World Bank's World Development Indicators. The three countries are chosen deliberately: Türkiye shares with Iran a comparable population size, geographical setting and human-resource base, while Saudi Arabia shares with Iran a vast hydrocarbon endowment, so that placing the two neighbours alongside Iran isolates the effect of political and economic decisions from the effect of underlying geography and resources. Using the Human Development Index and its component measures as an organising framework, the analysis finds that the three countries, which sat close together in 2005, have since diverged sharply. In 2005 Iran stood ahead of Türkiye on the Human Development Index and was closing on Saudi Arabia; but from the election of Mahmoud Ahmadinejad that same year, and through successive episodes of economic mismanagement and intensifying international sanctions, Iran's progress stalled and was overtaken, so that by 2023 both Saudi Arabia and Türkiye had entered the United Nations' Very High development category while Iran remained in the High category and had fallen behind on income, gender equality and economic complexity. Extending the analysis beyond the Human Development Index, to gross domestic product, sectoral composition, income inequality, exchange-rate regimes, external debt, sovereign wealth, subjective well-being and forecasts to 2035, corroborates this pattern. The report concludes that political and economic structure, rather than geography or resource endowment, is now the dominant explanation for the divergence observed since 2005.

detail.abstract: Critics have long charged that a casino drives the households nearest it into bankruptcy, and the claim now shapes local policy. Casinos have become a place-based development tool, sited deliberately in distressed communities: Virginia, for instance, recently authorized commercial casinos only in cities it designated as economically distressed. The evidence on whether casinos lead to more bankruptcies is dated and coarse, relying on data almost two decades old and measured at a county or state level, far too aggregated to isolate a casino's local effect (Anisfeld and Rosenthal-Kay 2025; Scavette 2023). We revisit the casino-bankruptcy link with spatial data fine enough to observe highly localized effects. We assemble a quarterly panel of consumer bankruptcy filings at the census-tract level for 2008:Q1 through 2026:Q1 and match it to the location and opening date of 1,130 U.S. casinos. Exposure is measured by the driving time from each tract's population centroid to the nearest casino. Using the partially pooled synthetic control estimator of Ben-Michael et al. (2022), we build each casino tract a counterfactual from distant but comparable tracts and trace the effect outward from the host tract. No specification we estimate shows a statistically significant increase in bankruptcy filings after a casino opens. At the host tract the estimates are positive but never significant; in the surrounding area they are predominantly negative. Where much earlier work reports a positive effect, the finer spatial scale that should make a casino's local influence clearest shows no increase at all.

detail.abstract: This paper provides a comparative methodological overview of four core quantitative frameworks used in modern financial economics: Supervised Classification, Unsupervised Clustering, Stochastic Simulation, and Agent-Based Modeling. Empirical placeholders are provided for implementation and visualization of results. The practical contribution of this work lies in demonstrating how cognitive and computational constraints shape model selection in real-world financial applications. While supervised and unsupervised methods offer tractable solutions for prediction and segmentation, stochastic and agent-based approaches are essential for capturing uncertainty and emergent behavior. By integrating these paradigms, institutions can develop more robust, adaptive risk management systems that remain valid across varying market regimes and data environments.

detail.abstract: Public open space (POS) assessment tools have proliferated across disciplines and application contexts, yet their results often remain difficult to compare. Existing research has largely attributed this divergence to differences in indicator selection, overlooking the broader assessment architecture within which indicators acquire meaning. This study examines why POS assessment tools diverge by conceptualizing them as layered sociotechnical sign systems. A systematic literature review identified 38 POS assessment tools, which were analyzed through structured content analysis. Twenty empirically derived attributes were mapped to a five-level semiotic framework comprising the empiric, syntactic, semantic, pragmatic, and social levels. The findings demonstrate that divergence is systematic rather than incidental and extends well beyond indicator content. At the empiric level, 57.9% of tools lack complete operational definitions, while 55.3% rely exclusively on subjective indicators. Structurally, 55.3% function as assessment frameworks rather than fully operational tools, reflecting substantial variation in procedural closure. Across all five semiotic levels, the cumulative interaction of measurement practices, structural organization, conceptual framing, intended application and institutional context generates cross-level structural misalignment that fundamentally constrains comparability. In response, this study proposes a semiotic compliance framework that specifies minimum documentation requirements for improving transparency, internal coherence, and interpretability without prescribing indicator standardization. The findings demonstrate that meaningful comparisons among POS assessment tools depend less on reducing indicator diversity than on explicitly aligning and documenting the multiple semiotic layers through which assessment systems generate meaning and support decision-making. The framework provides practical guidance for developing, evaluating, selecting, and comparing future POS assessment tools while preserving the contextual diversity required across different planning and governance settings.

title: An Attention Shock? Long-Term Evidence on Market Reactions to Mandatory CEO Pay Ratio Disclosures
affiliations: Monash University, Monash University - Department of Accounting and Monash University

detail.title: An Attention Shock? Long-Term Evidence on Market Reactions to Mandatory CEO Pay Ratio Disclosures
detail.abstract: We document a profound temporal decay in market reactions to mandatorily disclosed CEO-to-median-employee pay ratios from 2018 to 2024. During the inaugural year of the mandate, high-ratio firms experienced a significant decline in equity prices and institutional holdings. However, these market responses vanish in subsequent reporting cycles. We show that this longitudinal decay is driven by mutual adaptation. On the firm side, corporate boards adjust executive compensation at the extremes, causing disclosed pay ratios to converge towards the mean and a pooling equilibrium. On the market side, as the novelty of the disclosure fades, the initial attention shock dissipates when market participants withdraw attention. Collectively, our evidence demonstrates that a highly publicized transparency mandate can rapidly transition into a predictable corporate routine, resulting in a new long-term equilibrium where disclosures no longer provoke material market reactions.

detail.abstract: The circular economy is no longer an environmental luxury or a cosmetic line item in sustainability reports; it has become a matter of national security and state stability. This paper departs from a premise different from much of the existing Arabic-language literature, which tends to treat the circular economy as a "green economic opportunity" or an international environmental commitment. Instead, it argues that the circular transition-with organized recycling at its core-has become a sovereign survival condition for states that lack sufficient primary resource bases, chiefly countries of the Global South and non-oil Arab states. The paper traces the conceptual evolution of the circular economy, analyzes recent international data on critical mineral scarcity, the surge in electronic waste, and accelerating global resource consumption, reviews international governance frameworks-foremost among them Extended Producer Responsibility-and examines selected experiences from developing countries across Africa, Central Asia, and the Arab region. It concludes by proposing a new analytical framework, termed "Circular Sovereignty," as a practical decision-making tool for resourceconstrained states-one that redefines recycling not as a benign environmental behavior but as strategic infrastructure for economic security.

title: VTR-1: The Verifiable Track Record Standard — Enforcing Backtest Honesty Without Trusting the Issuer or Revealing the Strategy

detail.title: VTR-1: The Verifiable Track Record Standard — Enforcing Backtest Honesty Without Trusting the Issuer or Revealing the Strategy
detail.abstract:
Every correction for backtest overfitting depends on N, the number of strategies a researcher tried. The deflated Sharpe ratio needs it. So do multiple-testing haircuts and the probability of backtest overfitting. And N is supplied by the researcher. Nobody has ever been able to check it.

VTR-1 is an open standard that makes N a structural property of a cryptographic proof. The full set of candidate strategies is committed before evaluation, and N is the leaf count of that commitment. The winning result is forced in-circuit to be the maximum of the committed set. The anti-overfitting statistics are then recomputed inside a zero-knowledge proof, on committed price data, net of a committed cost floor. Any party can re-derive every asserted property in milliseconds against their own copy of the data. No trust is placed in the issuer at any step, and the strategy is never revealed.

The standard sets out three conformance levels, a verification procedure, and an adversary model naming seven attack classes. Its normative appendices pin the estimators, the fixed-point arithmetic and the commitment constructions closely enough that an independent implementation can reproduce a credential exactly. Forty-one numbered requirements let a conformance claim be contradicted. Nine known-answer conformance vectors are published with it, so a second implementation can be tested against something.

The standard is equally explicit about what it will not certify: future returns, capacity, market impact, and any strategy whose result depends on fills the committed data cannot justify. The reference implementation's first published verdict refused its own author's flagship strategy, deflated below significance and published permanently.

Published under CC BY 4.0. Anyone may implement it, including competitors of its steward.

title: Worker Mobility, Workforce Composition, and Employer Power
affiliations: , Charles H. Dyson School of Applied Economics of Management, Cornell University and Centre for Advanced Financial Research and Learning

detail.title: Worker Mobility, Workforce Composition, and Employer Power
detail.abstract: This paper studies worker mobility as a source of employer power. Our monopsony model shows that less mobile workers face larger markdowns because they supply labor less elastically; when improved outside options induce mobile workers to leave, the rising share of less-mobile workers raises source firms' average markdowns. We test this mechanism using India's National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (NREGA), which creates rural jobs without changing transport costs. We exploit its rollout across districts and nationally representative manufacturing data to estimate plant-level markdowns and NREGA's effects on manufacturing labor markets. Average effects are essentially zero, but the effects are concentrated among firms with low ex ante labor productivity. Relative to firms with initially high labor productivity, the program reduces employment at firms with initially low labor productivity by 9.8% and increases their markdowns by 10.5% and MRPL by 10.3%, while leaving wages unchanged. Effects are more pronounced among production workers and urban plants in districts with larger pre-treatment in-migrant shares, supporting the selective mobility mechanism.

title: The Joint Asymptotic Distribution of the Sharpe Ratio and Value at Risk Estimators: Efficiency versus Robustness

detail.title: The Joint Asymptotic Distribution of the Sharpe Ratio and Value at Risk Estimators: Efficiency versus Robustness
detail.abstract: We derive the joint asymptotic distribution of the Sharpe ratio and Value at Risk estimators under IID Gaussian returns for two constructions of the VaR: the empirical α-quantile and the parametric Gaussian quantile. The choice between estimators reduces to a pure efficiency-robustness trade-off. Under correct specification the relative efficiency of the parametric estimator grows from about 1.9 at the 5 percent level to about 15 at the 0.1 percent level; under misspecification it becomes inconsistent and the coverage of its confidence ellipse collapses and becomes biased, while the empirical quantile remains correctly centered at the nominal level, as our Monte Carlo experiments confirm.

title: Strategy-Proof Social Choice Correspondences for Conditional Expected Utility Maximizers *
affiliations: Universidad Complutense de Madrid

detail.title: Strategy-Proof Social Choice Correspondences for Conditional Expected Utility Maximizers *

declarations.funderStatement: Financial support from Agencia Estatal de Innovacion, Ministerio de Ciencia, Innovacion, y Universidades (Proyectos PID2022-138706NB-100, PID-2023-151783NB- 100) is gratefully acknowledged.

detail.abstract: We study social choice functions that take preferences over sets as input, when voters evaluate sets according to conditional expected utility obtained from Bayesian updating of a common prior.While under a uniform prior both dictatorial and bidictatorial rules satisfy strategy-proofness and unanimity, we show that this multiplicity is a knife-edge case: for every non-uniform prior, dictatorship is the unique rule satisfying these properties. The argument links set-valued rules to random dictatorship and shows that the probability ratios imposed by non-uniform updating are incompatible with combining the top choices of multiple voters. We also characterize the admissible rules when voters hold heterogeneous subjective priors.

title: Posterior Contraction and Credible Interval Coverage for Quantile Neural Networks
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and George Mason University

detail.title: Posterior Contraction and Credible Interval Coverage for Quantile Neural Networks
detail.abstract: Generative Bayesian computation replaces posterior simulation by supervised learning of a transport map from a base measure to the posterior. When the map is a conditional quantile function estimated by a deep network trained under check loss, the method is density free and requires only the ability to simulate. What has been missing is a statement of what the resulting object estimates and how fast. We supply three results. First, a contraction theorem: the estimated posterior converges to the true posterior in Wasserstein-1 distance at rate N-β /(2β +d) up to logarithmic factors, where N is the number of training simulations, β the Hölder smoothness of the conditional quantile map and d = d s + 1 the dimension of the summary statistic augmented by the quantile level. The proof routes the check loss excess risk through Knight's identity to an L 2 bound and then to W 1 by the quantile representation of optimal transport on the line. Second, a coverage theorem: the equal-tailed credible interval read off the estimated quantile map has coverage error of the same order, with a constant governed by the posterior density at the endpoints, so that intervals are conservative or anticonservative according to the sign of the estimation bias there. Third, a lower bound of N-β /(2β +d s) over the same class, which does not match the upper bound: the two differ by exactly one dimension, the quantile level, and we set out why our argument cannot close the gap and what would. We also isolate the term that does not vanish: when the summary statistic is not sufficient, all three results bound the distance to the summary posterior, and the gap to the full posterior is a fixed information loss that no amount of training removes. A numerical study on a conjugate model confirms contraction and coverage convergence but attains an empirical exponent of 0.21 rather than the 1/2 available for an analytic target, which we attribute to optimisation error rather than to the theory, and we say why.

title: Economic Integration Agreements and Growth: Dynamic Evidence from Switching Treatments
affiliations: University of Southern California - Department of Economics, Portland State University - Department of Economics and

detail.title: Economic Integration Agreements and Growth: Dynamic Evidence from Switching Treatments
detail.abstract: We estimate the dynamic growth effects of changes in Economic Integration Agreements using a 1990-2023 country panel and a heterogeneity-robust difference-in-differences estimator for multivalued, nonabsorbing treatments. Growth does not respond significantly in the switch year but rises by about 3 percentage points one year later. Four placebo estimates are individually and jointly insignificant, and the result is stable across alternative control groups, common-switcher, sample, and leave-one-out checks. The evidence points to delayed gains from major bloc-based integration episodes.

title: Disagreement, Memory, and the Fall into Deflation

detail.title: Disagreement, Memory, and the Fall into Deflation
detail.abstract: This paper shows that the dispersion of household beliefs can carry an economy from the inflation target into the deflationary trap, with the average expectation unmoved. In existing accounts of long deflations, fundamental forces explain the pressure on the policy rate while sunspot equilibria explain the economy's stay at the deflationary steady state. The path between the two steady states is what neither explains, because it enters those accounts as a coordination event drawn with an exogenous probability. Our mechanism runs on forecast selection. Households copy whichever forecasts of output, inflation, and the interest rate best match the historical record, weighting each component by the precision of its observation. The interest rate is the decisive component, because the bound censors its record on one side. Because prescriptions below the floor are recorded at the floor, pessimistic rate forecasts escape the penalty that optimistic ones pay. A mean-zero scattering of beliefs then starts a descent while the policy rate is still positive. Two quantities decide whether the descent completes: the dispersion of beliefs relative to the room above the floor and the length of the record of tenure at the target. Long memory filters the scattering out, while short memory lets selection carry the economy into the trap where the record then holds it.

title: Structural Dependency in the Global Economy: A System Dynamics Approach to Imperialism and Decolonization

detail.title: Structural Dependency in the Global Economy: A System Dynamics Approach to Imperialism and Decolonization

declarations.funderStatement: Leadership for the Ecozoic

detail.abstract: Imperial-colonial relations between core and peripheral countries persist through the contemporary architecture of trade, finance, and ecological extraction. This paper reconceptualizes global dependency as an emergent property of interacting macro-financial and ecological feedbacks that systematically reproduce debt, extraction, and constrained sovereignty in the Global South, rather than a transitional stage. Drawing on dependency theory, ecologically unequal exchange, and world-systems analysis, it develops a qualitative system dynamics framework, using Causal Loop Diagrams, modeling the global economy as a complex adaptive system structured by asymmetric power. Focusing on a stylized peripheral economy's balance of payments, the analysis maps how structural current account deficits, boom-and-bust cycles, illicit financial flows, financial speculation, external monetary pressures, and asymmetric institutions interact to generate persistent debt, ecological depletion, and constrained policy autonomy. These mechanisms exhibit nonlinearity, dominant reinforcing feedback, path dependence, co-evolution, multiple non-stable equilibria, and endogenous instability, challenging orthodox equilibrium assumptions. This perspective unifies trade, financial, and ecological dependencies into a single feedback architecture, identifying structural leverage points rather than parametric fixes. Building on this, the paper advances a decolonization pathway reframing delinking, anti-imperialist degrowth, and post-development as complementary interventions targeting trade/financial loops, institutional structures, and the values reproducing extractive demand, toward sovereign, just, socioecologically sustainable wellbeing.

title: Climate Action Justice
affiliations: University of California, Irvine and

detail.title: Climate Action Justice
detail.abstract:
California is widely regarded as a leader in climate policy. Questions remain, however, over whether state mandates for climate and environmental justice meaningfully translate into equitable planning and implementation, reduced health disparities, and improvements in quality of life among disadvantaged communities and vulnerable populations. Climate Action Justice examines that tension through a systematic review of General Plans and Climate Action Plans (CAPs) prepared by local governments across Southern California and the San Joaquin Valley.

In addition to providing comprehensive metric data for CAP and General Plan documents for over 500 jurisdictions and communities, the report is, to our knowledge, the first to analyze the content of unincorporated community planning documents, highlighting a crucial, neglected area of climate planning. We also enable comparison across jurisdictions, counties, and regions on matters of importance to climate planning, including equity, justice, language access, community engagement, plan alignment with state laws and policies, and implementation for the purpose of reducing disparities in adaptive capacity.

Our findings reveal a persistent disconnect between climate legislation, local planning, and environmental justice commitments across hundreds of jurisdictions in two of the state’s critical regions. General Plans and Climate Action Plans often fall short, specifically in recognitional and restorative justice, meaningful community engagement, alignment with legal requirements, and the ability to reduce persistent disparities in climate adaptive capacity.

Recent legislative developments demonstrate California’s growing recognition of climate justice concerns. However, without structural integration with and legal mandates for local climate action planning processes that mirror SB 1000’s requirements for environmental justice elements in general plans, these reforms will remain fragmented and of limited effectiveness. Updating CAPs to reflect evolving statutory mandates, strengthening context-specific vulnerability assessments under SB 379, investing in rural workforce infrastructure, embedding robust community engagement across stages of planning practice, and building an infrastructure by which local governments can understand, address, track, and reduce unequal adaptive capacities across multiple climate resilience cycles are necessary first steps.

title: Energy Law: The Legal Framework for Powering a Nation

detail.title: Energy Law: The Legal Framework for Powering a Nation
detail.abstract:
Energy is more than electricity; it is the strategic resource that drives economic growth, security, and infrastructure. Energy Law is the cluster of constitutional, commercial, environmental, tax, and contract rules that regulate the exploration, production, transportation, distribution, and use of petroleum, electricity, renewables, and emerging sources like hydrogen and nuclear.

In Nigeria, Energy Law aims to achieve availability, accessibility, affordability, and acceptability. Yet Nigeria faces a paradox: as Africa’s largest oil producer, it suffers grid instability, fuel import dependence, and energy poverty, however, the Petroleum Industry Act, 2021 and the Electricity Act, 2023 have improved bankability and allowed decentralized solutions like solar mini-grids for rural areas, challenges of cost, liquidity, and regulatory alignment remain. 

The energy value chain runs from upstream exploration, to midstream transport and storage, to downstream refining and marketing. At each stage, the law answers: who owns, who licenses, who prices, and who is liable. 

Globally, Energy Law is shifting through the Energy Transition toward Net Zero, cleaner energy, and a Just Transition that balances climate goals with equity.

title: Overreaction to AI Platform Scale
affiliations: University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business

detail.title: Overreaction to AI Platform Scale
detail.abstract: Many search problems in economics involve selecting an alternative based on a noisy signal of quality. In such settings, there is a core tradeoff between the scale of search and the signal fidelity. Guided by recent theory from Liang (2026), we conduct two experiments to investigate whether consumers internalize this core tradeoff. Subjects choose between an AI search technology and "in-person" search. We find that subjects substantially overreact to scale: even when scale has essentially no effect on AI value, AI adoption rises by 20 percentage points. Strikingly, this overreaction persists when subjects are informed about the AI platform's value.

title: Economic Structure and Peace Theory: How Sectoral Concentration and Inflation Influence the Possibility of Conflict 1
affiliations: and Charles University

detail.title: Economic Structure and Peace Theory: How Sectoral Concentration and Inflation Influence the Possibility of Conflict 1
detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether different parts of the economic structure of states can condition the probability of their involvement in violent conflict. While the main literature focuses on the relation between regime types and war or on natural resource dependence, few studies analyze the role of the general productive structure. Using a country-year panel dataset covering 247 countries over 64 years, merging the Uppsala Conflict Data Program (UCDP) and the World Development Indicators (WDI), a two-way fixed effects model estimates the impact of productive sectoral concentration, resource rents, inflation, GDP per capita, and economic closure on conflict incidence and intensity. The results indicate that inflation has a weak positive association during shocks, and most importantly, that productive concentration (HHI of value added) is negatively associated with the probability of internal conflict at a three-year lag, though the result weakens under multiple-testing corrections. This last finding provides the first suggestive evidence that sectoral concentration of the economic structure can influence the causes that induce internal conflict independently of political regime, challenging the assumption that concentrated economic systems necessarily breed internal instability.

title: The Best of Both Worlds? Comparative Framing in the Perception of Structured Financial Products
affiliations: University of Trier and University of Fribourg - Faculty of Economics and Social Science

detail.title: The Best of Both Worlds? Comparative Framing in the Perception of Structured Financial Products

declarations.ethicsApproval: The study was reviewed and approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Faculty of Management, Economics and Social Sciences at the University of Fribourg.

detail.abstract: Promotional descriptions of structured products often suggest that investors can benefit from the advantages of both bonds and stocks simultaneously. This impression arises from the selective comparison of realized payoffs to different reference instruments depending on the realized payoff. We argue that such comparative framing is not merely a marketing device, but rather a natural consequence of how investors evaluate these products given their modular design. Using experimental evidence for three commonly used product types, we show that investors systematically adjust their reference instrument to facilitate favorable investment evaluations. This pattern emerges even in the absence of suggestive product descriptions. Moreover, stronger comparative framing is associated with a higher perceived attractiveness of the products. Our findings suggest that comparative framing influences the evaluation of structured products and may contribute to their popularity by obscuring the underlying risk-return trade-off.

title:
The Fear of being Replaced: 
AI Exposure and Corporate Debt Maturity
affiliations: , Alma Mater Studiorum University of Bologna and University of Bologna - Department of Management

detail.title:
The Fear of being Replaced: 
AI Exposure and Corporate Debt Maturity
detail.abstract: This study examines whether firms' exposure to artificial intelligence (AI) affects corporate debt maturity. We argue that AI exposure constitutes a novel source of technological uncertainty, as it can reshape firms' competitive environment, intensify concerns about future industry disruption, and make long-horizon cash flows more difficult to evaluate. Using a sample of 1,759 U.S. listed firms over the 2015-2024 period, we find that greater AI exposure is associated with a higher proportion of short-term debt. The results remain robust to alternative specifications, alternative debt maturity proxies, and a placebo test. This relationship seems to be partially mitigated by firms' AI investment, proxied by the share of AI-skilled human capital within the workforce. Furthermore, we show that AI exposure is positively associated with the cost of debt, consistent with the view that creditors price an AI-related uncertainty premium. Cross-sectional tests show that the maturity-shortening effect is concentrated among intangible-intensive firms, where AI exposure exacerbates the opacity of the underlying asset base and compounds the difficulty of long-horizon credit assessment. We identify AI exposure as a new determinant of corporate debt maturity and show that the financial consequences of AI extend beyond labor markets and firm strategy to corporate financing choices.

title: Antitrust in the Quasi-Verse

detail.title: Antitrust in the Quasi-Verse
detail.abstract:
"Public" hospitals are being operated like private entities and are monopolizing healthcare markets, all while claiming immunity from state and federal antitrust laws. Scholarship has long framed hospital ownership as a binary choice between public and private ownership. Left unexplored are the various categories of public or government-owned hospitals. This article is the first to survey the structure, purpose, governance, and powers of the "quasi-verse"-so-called "quasi-corporations" that have both governmental and private attributes and are created by the local government to own and operate hospitals. Quasi-corporations look and function like private hospitals because power is delegated to independent boards that operate the hospitals, yet they retain governmental powers. This opens the possibility that these entities are exploiting governmental powers without meaningful oversight or accountability to voters. 

One such power is Parker immunity, a state power that can shield other governmental and private actors' anticompetitive behavior from federal and state antitrust scrutiny. This article reveals that quasi-corporations that operate hospitals harm competition through anticompetitive mergers and monopolization, yet are effectively immune from antitrust laws, adding fuel to the already troubling trend of rapid hospital consolidation, which impacts healthcare access, quality, and prices, particularly in rural and other underserved areas. This article outlines a path for a more restrained application of Parker immunity and offers enforcement recommendations for federal and state antitrust enforcers and state legislatures to mitigate antitrust concerns arising from quasi-corporations that own and operate hospitals.

title: Permanent Climate Change and GDP
affiliations: Stanford Graduate School of Business, University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School and Stanford

detail.title: Permanent Climate Change and GDP
detail.abstract: We examine internal migration within the United States to assess whether climate change will lead to lower economic growth. Because a mover experiences a persistent change in climate exposure, internal migration offers a useful setting for evaluating whether permanent warming generates large income losses, a question that the existing literature has addressed using temporary weather variation. We find that moves to warmer states and metropolitan areas are associated with marginally lower earnings. The estimated gradients are at least an order of magnitude smaller than even conservative existing estimates of the effect of climate change on economic activity, and a revealed preference for warmer destinations suggests they are an upper bound on a pure productivity penalty. Our findings suggest that research relying on temporary weather shocks to estimate the consequences of permanent warming may overstate the economic costs.

title: Liquidity for Transformation: Bank Credit and Firms' AI Adoption
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Federal Reserve Board of Governors, Carnegie Mellon University and Federal Reserve Board of Governors

detail.title: Liquidity for Transformation: Bank Credit and Firms' AI Adoption
detail.abstract: We study the role of bank credit in firms' adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), combining U.S. supervisory loan-level data with firm-level AI-related job postings. We find a two-way association between bank credit and AI adoption: greater bank credit predicts subsequent adoption, while adoption is followed by more credit at lower spreads, primarily through credit lines. Adopters also exhibit lower credit-line utilization. To address endogeneity in the effect of AI adoption on credit, we instrument for adoption using firms' predetermined workforce exposure to generative AI interacted with the release of ChatGPT. We show that this credit expansion crowds out lending to non-adopters, occurs without evidence of superior information production about AI adopters, and is concentrated among banks specializing in this segment. Overall, our findings suggest that banks facilitate AI adoption by providing precautionary liquidity through credit lines during firms' transformation.

title: Preservation vs. Monetization: A Microeconomic Analysis of Capital Allocation and Heritage Commercial Viability in Al-balad, Jeddah under Vision 2030
affiliations: Independent Research Project

detail.title: Preservation vs. Monetization: A Microeconomic Analysis of Capital Allocation and Heritage Commercial Viability in Al-balad, Jeddah under Vision 2030
detail.abstract: This paper tackles one of the fundamental questions of microeconomic research: How to crowd in private investment in an urban heritage zone when the traditional commercial real estate measures suggest that the market is doomed to fail, even if it is rescued by sovereign capital? The short run asset return indicator (𝑘 =0.00986) computed using the Saudi Public Investment Fund's (PIF) 18.75 billion SAR investment in Al Balad, Jeddah, through the Al Balad Development Company (BDC) is highly conservative in the terms of static multiplier analysis. In this analysis, it is shown that traditional accounting methods don't account for structural changes in markets caused by sovereign megaprojects. Historical preservation has important positive externalities, and free market competition will naturally under invest, resulting in a large deadweight loss where Marginal Private Benefit (MPB) is less than Marginal Social Benefit (MSB). Based on a spatial structural, this paper takes an analytical approach to examining the effects of sovereign absorption of infrastructure fixed costs that are prohibitive and non-recoverable on the private sector's Marginal Efficiency of Capital (MEC) curve. The key contribution of this framework is to show that the allocation of sovereign capital in 'heritage' districts should not be judged through a 'fiscal yield' approach, but rather its ability to remove structural failures of coordination and crowd in long term private commercial viability.

title: When Automation Concentrates Judgment: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Residual Decision Difficulty and Oversight Burden Following AI Adoption

detail.title: When Automation Concentrates Judgment: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Residual Decision Difficulty and Oversight Burden Following AI Adoption

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract:
Objective. Judgment Cost Theory predicts that automating prediction changes the composition of human decision work rather than shrinking it; its concentration and non-substitution propositions were tested against real deployments.

Methods. Random-effects meta-analysis following PRISMA 2020, registered on OSF after screening. Thirteen sources were searched to July 2026 for real-world evaluations of learned decision support reporting a human-side outcome and a comparison isolating adoption. Screening and extraction were duplicated by language-model reviewer-agents with human adjudication, and effects pooled with cluster-robust variance estimation. A post-deposit source re-verification of every computable effect size corrected the effect-size layer; the corrections are documented row by row, and the corrected estimates are the results.

Results. Eighty studies were included. The pooled association with residual concentration was positive but not statistically significant (d = +0.073 [−0.020, +0.166], p = .117); the theory-consistent signal was confined to binary decision outcomes (d = +0.181, p < .001) and to randomized designs (d = +0.125, p = .009), and the concentration funnel was significantly asymmetric, so small-study inflation cannot be excluded. Oversight burden showed no mean effect (d = −0.185, p = .381) but scaled with the irreducible uncertainty of the retained decision (b = +0.871, p = .002), independent of the share automated, though uncertainty is closely confounded with outcome measure type in this evidence base and the coefficient cannot be read as a clean moderator effect. The accountability moderator was not estimable: no low-accountability study yields a computable estimate. Heterogeneity was high (I² = 91% and 98%); certainty VERY LOW.

Conclusions. Adoption does not raise oversight on average; oversight scales with the irreducibility of the retained decision, not the amount automated. The pooled concentration estimate is small and positive but its confidence interval includes zero, leaving H1 inconclusive rather than confirmed or disconfirmed; the theory-consistent signal that does reach significance is confined to binary decision outcomes and randomized designs, at very low certainty and with a small-study caveat.

title: Ternary Republicanism: A New Institutional Framework for Global Governance

detail.title: Ternary Republicanism: A New Institutional Framework for Global Governance
detail.abstract:
Global governance confronts two intertwined structural crises. First, legitimacy deficits
erode the democratic authorization of international rules. Second, tax-base competition
drives a race to the bottom, depleting the fiscal capacity states need to supply public
goods. Neither dominant paradigm resolves this dual predicament: state-centric realism
cannot endogenize long-term cooperation, while market-centric institutionalism remains
vulnerable to regulatory capture by mobile capital. Multilateral reforms demanding near-
universal sovereign consensus—exemplified by the OECD Two-Pillar impasse—remain
stalled by prohibitively high political costs.
This paper proposes Ternary (Three-Pillar) Republicanism as an incremental institutional
framework. It builds on the principle of Popular Fiscal Sovereignty—the sovereign right
of citizens, as ultimate bearers of the tax burden, to authorize and decide on fiscal rules,
tax-base allocation, and institutional reforms. Three mutually reinforcing pillars translate
this principle into institutional design. Constitutional republicanism introduces bounded
judicial openness with professional guild constraints. Fiscal republicanism couples tax-
base sharing with material pledge requirements. Honor republicanism converts
reputational incentives into quantifiable, benefits-linked signals. Parameterized interfaces
outside core hard constraints allow heterogeneous legal traditions to connect without
converging on a single institutional model.
Rather than pursuing a supranational tax authority or a one-shot multilateral convention,
the framework advances through optional bilateral tax treaty protocols and mutual-
recognition arrangements. Publicly auditable performance signals drive Bayesian learning
and gradual diffusion. A complementarity performance function and a network adoption
model formalize its mechanism logic. Historical commercial institutions provide
mechanism-level existence proofs; contemporary anchors such as OECD Pillar Two and
international commercial courts illustrate partial implementations.
Positioned explicitly as a concept-derivation exercise under the normative premise of
cooperative prosperity, the paper makes three contributions. First, it reframes global
governance failures as a deficit across three complementary dimensions—judicial access,
tax-base allocation, and reputational incentives—none of which can function effectively
in isolation. Second, it provides a design template combining core hard constraints,
negotiable parameters, and material thresholds. Third, it develops a diffusion logic
showing how incremental reform via bilateral treaty add-ons can bypass the prohibitive
costs of universal multilateral consensus. The result is a bounded, negotiable, and
amenable to pilot implementation institutional design language for incremental global-
governance reform.

title: How Taking the Perspective of Imaginary Future Generations Changes the Direction of R&D Strategy and Employees’ Attitudes: Evidence from Future Design Practice in a Pharmaceutical Company
affiliations: The University of Osaka - Graduate School of Engineering, Nippon Shinyaku Co., LTD., The University of Osaka and Doshisha University

detail.title: How Taking the Perspective of Imaginary Future Generations Changes the Direction of R&D Strategy and Employees’ Attitudes: Evidence from Future Design Practice in a Pharmaceutical Company
detail.abstract: Taking a long-term perspective is a strict requirement for the pharmaceutical industry when designing R&D strategies and directions of innovation, making the training of individuals who can take on such tasks a critical challenge, and yet methodologies for such training remain underdeveloped. In this study, we investigated the effectiveness of adopting “imaginary future generations” (IFGs)—a proven mechanism for generating “futurability” in people—for R&D strategy design and personnel training in a pharmaceutical company. With the participation of employees of a Japanese pharmaceutical company, we conducted a discussion experiment exploring the topics of society and the company’s business in 2050, as well as essential R&D themes for future planning, both from the perspective of current generations and that of IFGs. The analysis results showed that when the IFGs perspective was adopted, there was a tendency to consider new R&D directions that view consumer perspectives and behavior changes in the future society in greater detail, resulting in an expansion of the company’s technologies into new fields of application, combining technologies of multiple fields, and more flexible responses to future environmental changes. The IFGs mechanism also changed the perceptions of participants. Specifically, the results demonstrated that the IFGs mechanism increases the motivation and initiative of individuals with respect to R&D and vision proposals. These results show that frameworks of discussion that incorporate the perspective of IFGs activate “futurability” that contributes to the design of new directions of R&D and innovation, and that IFGs are also effective in motivating employees.

title:
Vetting the Betting When High Stakes Replace Propaganda: 
A Prospect-theoretic Model of Electoral Influence through Prediction Markets

detail.title:
Vetting the Betting When High Stakes Replace Propaganda: 
A Prospect-theoretic Model of Electoral Influence through Prediction Markets
detail.abstract: We ask whether a campaign can influence an election more cheaply by taking positions in a prediction market than by spending on propaganda. The idea is to inject money on the favorite candidate (F), fattening the payout offered to anyone who bets on the trailing underdog (U), and to rely on the resulting financial stake to raise U's turnout. The objective, named plainly, is a form of indirect vote buying, and we analyze it as such. To keep the model simple, we assume the betting platform charges no fee, so that market odds are fair and the underdog's initial payout equals 1/p, with p the probability that U wins. We separate the mechanism into a behavior-free market layer and a behavioral decision layer. The market layer delivers an unwelcome result: the underdog payout is affine in the injection, so moving it materially requires money of the order of the whole pool-there is no leverage. The behavioral layer is more favorable to the strategy and formalizes the reflection effect of prospect theory: a partisan who already perceives U's likely defeat sits in the loss domain, where the value function is convex, becomes risk-seeking, and requires a far smaller payout to be drawn into a bet on U. The inducing payout falls monotonically in the voter's demoralization and, in the limit, the voter bets at any odds. We show, however, that the strategy rests on an unmeasured wager-to-turnout elasticity, that arbitrage leaks the subsidy, that success is self-limiting through the price, and that its fully effective form collapses into unlawful direct vote buying. A numerical illustration ties the pieces together.
