detail.abstract: This study develops an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI)-driven hybrid econometric-machine learning framework for nowcasting and forecasting Ghana's quarterly GDP, addressing the absence of a robust real-time forecasting system for macroeconomic policymaking. Using quarterly data from 2000Q1-2024Q4, the study develops and evaluates 29 standalone and hybrid econometric and machine learning models. Feature engineering and selection were applied to 30 high-frequency domestic and international indicators, identifying the 10 most significant predictors of GDP growth. The proposed FAVAR-XGBoost model emerged as the best-performing algorithm, achieving a Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 0.845 and an " # of 0.932, outperforming all benchmark econometric and standalone machine learning models. To address the "black-box" challenge associated with artificial intelligence, the study employs SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to quantify the contribution of each predictor to GDP forecasts, thereby enhancing model transparency and supporting evidence-based policy decisions. The study contributes to the literature by demonstrating the superiority of hybrid econometric-machine learning models for GDP nowcasting in data-constrained economies, developing a scalable framework for real-time macroeconomic surveillance, and advancing the application of explainable AI in macroeconomic forecasting. The findings suggest that hybrid models can substantially improve the accuracy, interpretability, and policy relevance of GDP nowcasts. It is recommended that the Bank of Ghana, the Ministry of Finance, and other central banks adopt the proposed FAVAR-XGBoost framework to strengthen real-time GDP monitoring and support timely monetary and fiscal policy decisions.

title: Driving on Unequal Exchange : Imperial Labour Transfers in the Global Automobile System and the True Speed of Car

detail.title: Driving on Unequal Exchange : Imperial Labour Transfers in the Global Automobile System and the True Speed of Car
detail.abstract: This paper revisits Ivan Illich's concept of "effective speed" by incorporating the global redistribution of embodied labour that sustains automobile systems. While existing estimates measure the time motorists must work to afford car use, they omit the labour performed abroad and transferred through ecological unequal exchange. We extend this framework by introducing an additional time component: the net embodied labour imported through global supply chains. Using multi-regional input-output analysis (EXIOBASE) combined with material flow data, we compute a corrected effective speed for 31 countries and disaggregate results by income decile. We show that automobile effective speed is partly the result of assymetric transfers. High-income countries gain up to 5 km/h through unequal exchange, while lower-income countries experience corresponding losses. The global median effective speed is approximately 15 km/h: for half of the world's motorists, the car does not outperform the bicycle. However, at the national level, we identify a mechanism of "imperial overcompensation": in net-importing countries, unequal exchange raises the effective speed of lower and middle income groups above what domestic redistribution alone would allow, and, absent this transfer, the car would fail to beat the bicycle well into the middle-income deciles of wealthy countries. These findings suggest that technological efficiency is a relational property of the world economy and that resistance to transport decarbonisation could reflect material interests structured by global labour transfers.

title: Foundations of Outcome Portfolio Theory

detail.title: Foundations of Outcome Portfolio Theory

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has ownership interests in privately held companies operating in wealth-management lending and lead generation. These companies did not fund the research and had no role in the analysis, preparation, or conclusions of this paper. The author declares no other competing interests.

detail.abstract:
Modern Portfolio Theory selects portfolios in coordinates of risk and return. This paper selects them in coordinates of wealth and time, using the continuous-time capital-allocation model throughout, with nothing added that the model forbids.

Under geometric Brownian motion, expected wealth grows at the arithmetic rate mu, while expected log wealth, median wealth, and the almost-sure long-run compound growth rate are governed by the geometric rate g = mu - (1/2)sigma^2. No positive-volatility portfolio has equal arithmetic and geometric rates (Proposition 1); the gap is (1/2)sigma^2, exact and known in advance.

An investor who responds by de-risking toward the portfolio whose arithmetic rate matches the geometric rate they are receiving generates a recursion whose only fixed point is cash; convergence is harmonic, which is why the descent cannot be felt from inside it (Proposition 2).

An investor who instead repeatedly re-levers so that each position's geometric rate matches the previous position's arithmetic promise generates a strictly increasing recursion that reaches an infeasible promise in finitely many steps: an arithmetic target no exposure can deliver (Proposition 3).

The recursion itself never passes the Kelly peak; persisting beyond its warning by discretionary escalation crosses first Kelly and then the zero-growth boundary, where the geometric rate is negative and wealth declines almost surely.

One spiral converges to cash in infinitely many steps and cannot be felt; the other reaches its warning in as few as one. A third response, doing nothing, pays (1/2)sigma^2 against the geometric rate every period, forever.

The response that is not a spiral requires a destination. This paper supplies one by adding two axioms: a goal (A1) and an admissibility boundary on ruin (A2), stated with a formal ruin event.

From these, together with the dynamics and financing freedom the continuous-time model already contains, the paper derives: a closed-form restoration exposure whose two roots are mirror images through the Kelly peak (Propositions 4-5); an unconstrained feasibility boundary mu >= 2sigma^2 that is the discriminant of the same quadratic, not an imposed condition (Proposition 6); the collapse of the entire geometry to one dimensionless parameter u = 2sigma^2/mu; the result that the utility level implied by the static capital-allocation choice is unattainable on the compounding frontier for every coefficient of risk aversion, while the through-time optimum exists at strictly less risk (Proposition 7); and a second-mover restoration rule whose wealth-to-benchmark ratio follows an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process whose conditional mean reverts toward mu/a, so that correct specification of the benchmark rate is required for centering at the benchmark, not for mechanical stability (Proposition 8).

The conjecture that recovery cancels the drag exactly in the stationary limit is tested and fails in its naive formulation: the positive-region stationary expectation of log relative wealth is negative at the tested calibrations, approximately -sigma^2/(4mu) in the small-variance regime. Recovery at that limit is partial, yet the same rule closes the arithmetic mean exactly at every horizon, E[R_t] = 1 (Proposition 9), and a strict Jensen argument proves that no nondegenerate positive policy closes the arithmetic and geometric functionals simultaneously (Proposition 10). The residual is qualitatively irreducible; its minimum attainable magnitude under admissibility constraints is the open problem the paper leaves behind. Simulation evidence for the operational rules is reported at the tier it earns.

As a slogan: Outcome Portfolio Theory is Modern Portfolio Theory plus a goal and an admissibility boundary. As a definition: Outcome Portfolio Theory takes the continuous-time capital-allocation model, re-expresses it in wealth-time coordinates, and adds A1 and A2.

detail.abstract: Felix Cohen showed that courts protected a trade name because they called it property, when in truth they called it property because they had decided to protect it. I apply his test to a word now doing a great deal of work in European law. An artificial intelligence system is called highrisk because Annex III lists it; the label comes off if the provider judges that his own system poses no significant risk; and the consequences of the label begin on whatever date the legislature appoints. As I write, that date has just been moved from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027. Nothing about any of these systems changed on the day the amendment took effect. What changed is what the word costs. My argument then departs from Cohen. He thought such words empty, and therefore a screen for policy. I say they are not weightless. They settle who must argue, and they settle it always in the same direction.

title: Skillsnti: The Skills that Sustain Everything Else: Developing Essential Human Competencies in the Era of Digital Transformation

detail.title: Skillsnti: The Skills that Sustain Everything Else: Developing Essential Human Competencies in the Era of Digital Transformation
detail.abstract:
The SkillsNTI Project represents a comprehensive initiative in applied research and educational transformation that systematizes the development of non technical skills (HNTI, by its Spanish acronym) as foundational pillars of professional performance. What are these essential non-technical skills? They constitute a set of socio-emotional and cognitive capabilities—many of which can be developed through structured training and practice—such as effective communication, active listening, empathy, emotional intelligence, emotional regulation, creative conflict resolution, problem-solving, creativity, adaptability, leadership, decision-making, teamwork, negotiation, resilience, lifelong learning, and critical thinking.
The HNTI methodology is structured around five essential competency domains: emotional and cognitive self-management, interpersonal and collaborative management, complex thinking and problem-solving, workplace and social commitment, and transferable and multifunctional competencies. These domains are directly linked to five procedural dimensions (5D): Discover, Develop, Challenge, Perform, and Deploy.
This innovative approach not only integrates empirical evidence gathered from diverse methodological sources but also provides practical, scalable tools for educators, trainers, and professionals across multiple sectors. SkillsNTI demonstrates that competencies traditionally labeled as "soft skills" can be systematically structured, measured, and transferred, transforming teaching learning processes into experiences of sustainable and measurable professional growth.

title: How Does New Information Influence Individuals' Uncertainty Beliefs?
affiliations: ,  and University of Muenster - Finance Center

detail.title: How Does New Information Influence Individuals' Uncertainty Beliefs?

declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the Fritz Thyssen Stiftung [Grant 20.21.0.023WW].

detail.abstract: Individuals use new information not only to update their expectations about future outcomes, but also to reassess how certain they are about these outcomes. While a large experimental literature examines biases in expectation updating, much less is known about how individuals update beliefs about uncertainty. A key reason is methodological: in the standard two-state balls-and-urns paradigm, changes in expected outcomes and changes in uncertainty cannot be separated because both are mechanically linked. To examine biases in uncertainty updating, we analyze belief formation in incentivized multi-state balls-and-urns experiments with three or more possible states of the world. In these settings, signals can change the dispersion of posterior beliefs independently of expected outcomes, allowing us to separately identify distortions in beliefs about uncertainty. We document three main findings. First, individuals systematically underreact to the impact of new information on posterior uncertainty. Second, this bias becomes stronger when signals carry greater information weight, implying particularly strong underreaction to highly informative evidence. Third, individuals insufficiently account for prior uncertainty, mirroring classic forms of base rate neglect in expectation updating. Moreover, we show that biased perceptions of uncertainty can spill over into expectation updating.

title: Apparent Continuity: Chartered Memory Drift and the Self-Concealing Authority of Unchanged Texts
affiliations: Epistria

detail.title: Apparent Continuity: Chartered Memory Drift and the Self-Concealing Authority of Unchanged Texts
detail.abstract: Organizations hold charters, covenants, constitutions, and policies that remain textually unchanged for years while the meaning under which they operate migrates substantially. Existing theory explains how such migration occurs: through the evolution of routines, the retention and loss of organizational memory, the taken-for-grantedness of institutionalized rules, and the divergence of policy from practice. It does not explain why an unchanged text continues to function as evidence of continuity after its operative meaning has moved. This paper names that condition apparent continuity and specifies the mechanism that produces it. Drawing a deliberate contrast with the constitutional doctrine of historical gloss (which explains how a recognized departure acquires legitimacy), it describes the complementary case, in which a departure ceases to be recognized as a departure at all. The central claim is that an unchanged authoritative text is not evidence that operative meaning has remained unchanged. Under the conditions specified here, its persistence is the mechanism by which operative continuity is falsely inferred. The endpoint normally supplied by institutional acceptance is instead supplied by documentary continuity. The paper specifies the mechanism, offers a means of detecting apparent continuity, and distinguishes the phenomenon from the neighboring accounts it can be mistaken for.

title: Monotonicity and Rigidity in Gaussian Inverse Regression: The One-Period Kyle Model Has a Unique Equilibrium
affiliations: Australian National University (ANU) - Research School of Economics and Brazilian School of Economics and Finance (FGV EPGE)

detail.title: Monotonicity and Rigidity in Gaussian Inverse Regression: The One-Period Kyle Model Has a Unique Equilibrium
detail.abstract: Let V and U be independent standard normal random variables. For Borel ϕ : R → R, let P ϕ be a version of the inverse regression P ϕ (y) = E[V | ϕ(V) + U = y] , and F ϕ (x) = E[P ϕ (x + U)] its Gaussian smoothing. We prove that ϕ(v) ∈ arg max x∈R xv-x F ϕ (x) , for every v ∈ R if and only if ϕ = id R , the identity function. This is the pointwise bestresponse condition of the normalised one-period Kyle insider trading model; consequently the affine equilibrium strategy of Kyle (1985) is unique amongst all strategies. This settles the uniqueness question for the one-period Gaussian Kyle model. The additional ingredient relative to the McLennan, Monteiro and Tourky (2017) analytic framework is probabilistic: an exchangeable pair, obtained by resampling the value from the market makers' posterior, whose balance identities, combined with a Gaussian inequality for monotone functions, make the posterior mean affine.

title: The Accommodation Subscription: Tiered Artificial Intelligence Accessibility, Reliance, and the Nondelegable Duty in Public Education

detail.title: The Accommodation Subscription: Tiered Artificial Intelligence Accessibility, Reliance, and the Nondelegable Duty in Public Education
detail.abstract: Captions, transcripts, and synthetic speech are auxiliary aids and services. On the major educational artificial intelligence platforms they are also priced. A rudimentary version of each is distributed at no cost, and the version that actually works for a disabled student sits inside a paid edition or a paid add-on that the school district must purchase separately. This article argues that the resulting arrangement violates Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act in the hands of the purchasing district, and Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act in the hands of the vendor, and that the two conclusions are independent of one another. The argument depends on no doctrinal reform. It rests on three settled propositions: that the duty of a public entity runs through its contractual and licensing arrangements and cannot be discharged by procurement; that an auxiliary aid must be effective rather than merely present; and that a covered entity may not impose the cost of nondiscriminatory treatment on the individuals who require it. A closing Part treats, as an alternative posture, the harder case of a vendor with no physical premises, which is reachable only on a functional reading of the statutory categories. The article then identifies the harm that tiered pricing produces over time. A student is given an aid, adapts to it, and organizes their participation around it, and the aid is then withdrawn when the district cannot absorb a price increase it did not set. That withdrawal, not the initial purchase, is the actionable event, and it is a lost educational opportunity in the exact sense that the Ninth Circuit preserved from the reach of Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller in Payan v. Los Angeles Community College District.

title: A Model-Agnostic Level-Set Approach for Prescriptive Analytics
affiliations: Business Administration & Economics and Julius-Maximilians-University Wuerzburg

detail.title: A Model-Agnostic Level-Set Approach for Prescriptive Analytics
detail.abstract: Data-driven approaches that leverage machine learning for stochastic optimization with contextual information ('prescriptive analytics') have received considerable attention in recent years. However, existing approaches often rely on the inherent properties of specific models or require problemspecific modifications and training. Motivated by this limitation, we propose a novel framework that allows practitioners to leverage any machine learning model for prescriptive analytics. We introduce a new class of kernel functions that measure similarity through proximity in the prediction space ('level-set approach'). The resulting kernel values can be integrated into existing data-driven optimization techniques that rely on sample weighting or kernel-based transformations. We establish asymptotic optimality under mild assumptions when our method is applied to weighted sample average approximation and demonstrate consistent translation of predictive into prescriptive performance through various numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world data. Our experiments show that using state-of-the-art models within our framework yields substantial cost reductions relative to existing benchmarks.

title: When is Training-Data Causation Identifiable in Generative Models? From Training Documents to Protected Works

detail.title: When is Training-Data Causation Identifiable in Generative Models? From Training Documents to Protected Works
detail.abstract: When a court asks whether a language model copied a training document, several questions get conflated: did the output match the document; would it have matched without that document; if many documents shared the same content, which is responsible; and is the matched material protected expression, or unprotectable fact and convention? Only the match is visible in the output. Protectability is settled by filtration, the legal step that removes unprotectable elements, and the two causal questions require a controlled experiment the deployed model alone cannot supply. This paper proves three results. First, an impossibility: no function of deployed-model outputs identifies a training document's causal contribution. Two behaviourally identical models can have arbitrarily different attribution, because the unobserved rest of the corpus confounds every estimate formed from outputs alone. The output preserves the copied content but not its provenance, so output-only attribution carries a known error rate that grows with redundancy. Second, controlled insertion at training time supplies the missing experiment: match rates with and without the document sharply bound the probability that the document was necessary and sufficient for the match (PNS). Under a monotonicity assumption, PNS and the separate probabilities of necessity and sufficiency all have closed forms. Third, copyright protects the work, not the training document. When a work is spread across many documents, per-document PNS can vanish while work-level PNS stays high, so document-level attribution under-attributes the protected work by construction. Intervening on all carriers of the work at once restores identification at the level the law protects, and when carriers are interchangeable it yields each document's Shapley share. Measuring the match after filtration restricts the causal question to protected expression, and an evidence map ties each legal or audit question to the causal quantity and evidence it requires.

title: Above the Law: Torture Accountability and Its Limits in U.S. Law
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Above the Law: Torture Accountability and Its Limits in U.S. Law
detail.abstract:
In the years following the September 11 attacks, the United States built one of the most extensive

legal architectures against torture of any nation and then constructed a global network of secret

prisons on top of it. The Central Intelligence Agency's Rendition, Detention, and Interrogation 1

program subjected roughly one hundred detainees to what officials called “enhanced

interrogation techniques,” including waterboarding, at a time when the United States remained

bound by an absolute, non-derogable prohibition on torture. That prohibition is widely 2

understood in international law as jus cogens, literally, “compelling law” - a peremptory norm

from which no state may derogate, even in wartime or a declared national emergency. Yet history

complicates the tidiness of that principle.

title: Britain and the United States Motion Picture Industry

detail.title: Britain and the United States Motion Picture Industry
detail.abstract: The United Kingdom is the most important foreign base of the United States film and television industry. American studios supply capital, intellectual property, and worldwide distribution, and Britain supplies crews, stages, locations, visual effects, post-production, and production incentives. This paper measures that relationship and applies it to the proposed acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery by Paramount Skydance. Drawing on British Film Institute inward-investment data and standard multiplier analysis, I estimate the total annual benefit to the United Kingdom from American studios and streamers at £17 to £21 billion, comprising direct production spending, indirect and induced activity, and permanent operations. Britain is also one of the most valuable theatrical markets in the world for an American film. The paper then asks what a combination of two of the five remaining major studios would mean for that relationship. A merger removes an independent buyer of scripts, stages, crews, and talent, and the combined company would carry roughly USD 79 billion in debt against roughly USD 3 billion in free cash flow. Those two facts create strong incentives to reduce output and employment. Britain, which holds more of the combined company's people and facilities than any country outside the United States, has the most to lose.

detail.abstract: Hybrid platforms disadvantage third-party sellers through the platform fee and self-preferencing, and regulators have worried that constraining either instrument may intensify the other. We model a platform that chooses both instruments and find the opposite: single-instrument regulation is effective because the instruments are strategic complements, and regulating either instrument curbs the other. We also find that the two instruments achieve what monopolization achieves, higher prices and reduced consumer welfare, while passing every conventional antitrust test.

detail.abstract: Private philanthropic organisations have become influential actors in African agricultural governance, supplying finance, technical expertise, policy support and institutional partnerships alongside governments and development agencies. Existing scholarship has examined philanthrocapitalism in relation to productivity, biotechnology and development outcomes, but less attention has been paid to how these interventions reshape the relationship between institutional capacity and food-system sovereignty. This paper develops the concept of conditional dependency to explain how external support can expand the operational capacity of African agricultural institutions while simultaneously constraining their long-term autonomy. Using the Alliance for a Green Revolution in Africa (AGRA) and Kenya's Agricultural Sector Transformation and Growth Strategy (ASTGS) as core illustrations, the study analyses organisational reports, government documents, independent evaluations and peer-reviewed literature. Four mechanisms-financial asymmetry, institutional embeddedness, epistemic asymmetry and technological asymmetry-explain how dependency may emerge even when partnerships generate developmental benefits. The paper argues that the central question is not whether philanthrocapitalist interventions succeed or fail, but whether externally supported capabilities become self-sustaining or remain reliant on external finance, expertise and governance structures. The expanded SSRN version provides additional theoretical context, historical background and policy implications for African technological sovereignty.

detail.abstract: Bank mergers erode consumer welfare in communities where acquirers keep branches open. Across 260,523 geolocated reviews of U.S. bank branches matched to 862 mergers between 2014 and 2024, ratings fall 14% at completion and average about 10% lower post-merger. Branch closures do not explain the decline; integration does. The damage is deepest at small branches and in small markets. Complaints concentrate on systems and staffing at regional acquirers, and on service interactions and bureaucratic delays at large ones. Deposit growth falls a further 9 to 11 percentage points at branches where customers voiced dissatisfaction beforehand. Where they had been satisfied, customers stay, and regional acquirers go on to price mortgages above their local market.

title: The Burden of Green: Why the State Must Transition Before the Citizen
affiliations: S.K.J Law College

detail.title: The Burden of Green: Why the State Must Transition Before the Citizen
detail.abstract: India is navigating a complex transition toward sustainable energy and reduced reliance on imported crude oil. However, the regulatory execution disproportionately offloads the economic, financial, and operational risks of this macro-level shift onto private consumers. From the mandated rollout of ethanol-blended petrol (E20) without adequate underground storage infrastructure to arbitrary age-based vehicle scrapping policies and forced electric vehicle adoption, citizens face systemic threats to their fundamental rights. This paper presents a constitutional and regulatory critique of India's green transition frameworks. By analyzing real-world operational failures, including phase-separation contamination at fuel stations and recent consumer forum jurisprudence holding automakers liable for E20 incompatibility, this article demonstrates how state policy infringes upon Articles 14, 19(1)(g), and 21 of the Constitution of India. Furthermore, it exposes the state's reliance on a judicial "fait accompli" doctrine, evidenced in the Supreme Court's 2025 recall of its own ban on retrospective environmental clearances, to shield arbitrary mandates behind irreversible economic investments. The paper concludes by proposing a top-down regulatory model requiring decarbonization of state fleets and heavy logistics prior to imposing coercive obsolescence on private individuals.

title: Perishable Inventory Control with Markov Chain Choice-Induced Issuance: Policy Design and Performance Bounds
affiliations: , City University of Hong Kong and University of British Columbia

detail.title: Perishable Inventory Control with Markov Chain Choice-Induced Issuance: Policy Design and Performance Bounds
detail.abstract: Managing perishable inventory requires balancing expiration risk, stockout costs, and customers' heterogeneous preferences regarding product age. While classical models often assume deterministic issuance rules such as FIFO or LIFO, many retail settings do not permit such control. Instead, the sequence of which age units are sold is shaped by customers' sequential choices, substitution behavior, search frictions, and specific preferences for product age. We study a finite-horizon periodic-review lost-sales inventory problem for a single perishable product with a fixed lifetime. Inventory is tracked by remaining lifetime, and customers arrive sequentially, each choosing among the available remaining-lifetime categories or leaving without purchase. We model this behavior using a Markov chain choice model (MCCM), which captures stochastic search and substitution across age categories and includes deterministic FIFO and LIFO issuance as special cases. Viewing remaining-lifetime categories as freshness-differentiated products turns the inventory available to customers into an endogenous assortment: it is shaped by ordering, aging, disposal, and prior customer choices rather than selected directly by the retailer. Using this endogenous-assortment perspective, we develop a fluid-guided joint ordering and disposal policy (JOD). The policy translates a target nested set of remaining-lifetime categories into an implementable age-management policy by ordering fresh units and using disposal to control the future age profile. The associated fluid relaxation upper-bounds the transformed revenue of any feasible policy and motivates the target inventory structure. Under the multinomial logit model, we prove an additive largemarket optimality-gap bound for JOD when the planning horizon T and fixed lifetime m are fixed and the arrival rate grows. For arbitrary MCCMs, we establish an asymptotic cost-ratio guarantee for the best revenue-ordered target under explicit cost and horizon conditions. When holding cost is zero, JOD simplifies to ordering only fresh units and carrying all nonexpired leftovers, and we obtain an additive large-market bound for arbitrary MCCMs without revenue-ordered approximation loss. We further embed FIFO, LIFO, and threshold search within the MCCM framework, characterize conditions under which revenue-ordered targets are fluid-optimal, and derive sharper additive bounds for these structured cases. Numerical experiments show that age-sensitive control can substantially outperform age-blind base-stock policies, especially when age-specific stockouts lead to customer abandonment.

title: Geopolitical Risk and Cross-Asset Implied Volatility: Evidence from Equity, Oil, and Gold Options

detail.title: Geopolitical Risk and Cross-Asset Implied Volatility: Evidence from Equity, Oil, and Gold Options
detail.abstract: This paper examines how geopolitical shocks reprice risk across equity, oil, and gold options markets through both aggregate implied volatility and full volatility surface distortion. Using end-of-day options data on equities, gold, and oil and analyzing systematically identified geopolitical events through geopolitical newspaper coverage frequency, I document statistically significant but structurally distinct responses across the three asset classes. Equity volatility is uniform and risk is not priced into any specific region of the surface. Oil exhibits the most consistent surface distortion, concentrated in the deep out-of-the-money wings. Gold shows the largest response and responds more strongly to anticipated threats than realized acts. All three assets deflate after a geopolitical event consistent with the popular buy-the-rumor, sell-the-news mechanism. The most novel finding is that gold's structurally call-skewed surface intensifies sharply on event days, revealing that investors express safe-haven demand through upside call buying rather than downside put protection. Finally, shock severity above the identification threshold adds little explanatory power, consistent with geopolitical fear operating as a binary regime switch rather than a continuous variable.

Artificial Intelligence in Financial Risk Management

Artificial Intelligence in Financial Risk Management 
Prediction, Automation, and Systemic Exposure in Modern Markets

detail.abstract: This monograph examines how artificial intelligence is reshaping financial risk management across prediction, credit underwriting, trading, and systemic risk. It traces the evolution of risk modeling from classical statistics through machine learning to large language models, arguing that each successive era trades interpretability for predictive flexibility in ways existing governance frameworks were not built to address. Distinct chapters examine AI-driven market prediction and algorithmic trading, credit risk modeling and the proxy-discrimination problem, and the emergence of systemic risk from correlated AI adoption across otherwise unrelated institutions — a risk category not yet well captured by either microprudential or macroprudential supervision. The book surveys the current regulatory landscape, including the EU AI Act's treatment of credit scoring as high-risk, evolving Basel Committee guidance, and U.S. model risk management standards, identifying specific gaps: the absence of system-wide foundation-model dependency monitoring, fragmented cross-border coordination, and asymmetric regulatory maturity between lending and trading applications. Four illustrative case studies ground the analysis in concrete institutional scenarios. The central argument is that AI's role in prediction must be governed separately from its role in decision, and that governance capacity should be treated as a co-requirement of AI adoption in finance, not a follow-on concern.

title: Factors Influencing the Adoption of Forensic Accounting Practices Among Financial Institutions In Nigeria: The Diffusion of Innovation Theory (DIT) Perspective
affiliations: De Montfort University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Factors Influencing the Adoption of Forensic Accounting Practices Among Financial Institutions In Nigeria: The Diffusion of Innovation Theory (DIT) Perspective

keywords: Observability and Diffusion of Innovation Theory

detail.abstract: Purpose-The study focuses on the financial institutions in Nigeria from the lens of diffusion of innovation theory (DIT). It aims to investigate the drivers influencing the adoption of forensic accounting practices among financial institutions in the Nigerian Financial Sector. Design/methodology/approach-Data were collected via survey questionnaire and confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modelling were used to examine the model fit and the hypotheses, respectively. SMARTPLS 4.0 software was used for data analysis. Quantitative analysis was carried out to examine how the five drivers of innovation from organisational context influence the behaviour decision to adopt forensic accounting practices. Findings-This study found that Relative Advantage, Complexity, Trialability and Observability were all significant drivers of adoption of Forensic Accounting Practices in the Nigeria Financial Industry. Furthermore, the study found that while Observability has the strongest influence on the decision to adopt forensic accounting practices in the Nigerian Financial Industry, Complexity has the weakest influence. However, the study found no significant relationship between the driver of Compatibility and Adoption of Forensic Accounting Practices. Research limitations/implications-Data collection in financial institutions is always difficult because of their reluctant to give away information. Many of the participants were sceptical of the mission of the researcher due to the sensitivity of the questions being asked thereby limiting the number of samples collected. The importance of forensic accounting has grown in tandem with the rise in financial crimes. By implication, forensic accounting adoption is crucial in the implementation of proactive measures to prevent, detect and mitigate fraud in the Nigerian Financial Sector and management must recognise this importance. Originality/value-To the best of this researcher's knowledge, there has been no study conducted to investigate the drivers influencing the adoption of forensic accounting practices in the context of financial institutions in the Nigerian Financial Sector and from the theoretical lens of diffusion of innovation theory.

title:

A Benchmark for Auditing AI-generated Trading Strategies with a Reference Implementation on Indian Equities
detail.abstract:
A language model that writes trading strategies is a machine for manufacturing plausible
backtests, and the two failure modes that make those backtests worthless—lookahead bias
and multiple testing—are precisely the two a naive evaluation cannot see. We release
AlphaAudit: a benchmark for measuring whether an auditor can tell, in advance
and out of sample, which machine-generated strategies are worth acting on.
It comprises a survivorship-free Indian equity environment, a verified transaction-cost
model, leaky and clean fixture suites, an audited 1,550-candidate corpus, a frozen one-shot
evaluation protocol, and the reference implementation reported below.

detail.abstract:
Cybersecurity has become a major problem for organizations, which have responded with

employee-facing policies such as security trainings, firewalls, and rules about new technologies.

These policies work best when employees believe the threat they address is real. Across six

experiments (total N = 2,893), we identify two routes through which organizational policy

decisions can undermine this belief, and show that each can be attenuated. When solutions are

imposed in restrictive ways, employees experience psychological reactance and deny that the

threat is serious: a firewall that blocks popular apps (versus an education policy; Study 1) and a

boss mandating training attendance (versus offering a choice; Study 2) both increased denial

through heightened reactance. Yet preserving autonomy within a mandate, letting employees

choose how to complete a required training rather than dictating it, reduced both reactance and

denial (Study 3). When policies are removed, employees infer that the organization has

concluded the threat is not serious and adopt that verdict themselves: employees recalling a lifted

(versus kept) cybersecurity policy (Study 4) and participants imagining a company lifting a

generative AI ban (Study 5) reported greater denial. Yet reaffirming that the risk remained

serious while lifting the ban weakened this inference and reduced denial (Study 6). We discuss

how organizations can impose, and sunset, risk-management policies without teaching

employees to dismiss the threat.

title: Humanitarian Intervention and Post-war Outcomes
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Humanitarian Intervention and Post-war Outcomes
detail.abstract: This article tests a central claim of the Fraser Theory of Post-Colonial Intervention (FTPI): that the legitimacy of humanitarian military intervention cannot be assessed by intention or immediate battlefield outcome alone, but must be judged against the responsibilities an intervening power assumes once it has transformed a political society. FTPI's central maxim that responsibility is proportional to transformation predicts that interventions producing deep political and institutional change generate correspondingly extensive obligations of reconstruction, accountability, and stewardship, and that failure to meet those obligations produces long-term fragility regardless of short-term military or humanitarian success. The article tests this prediction through a structured comparison of six post-Cold War interventions (Bosnia, Kosovo, Afghanistan, Iraq, Libya, and Syria), classified along FTPI's six-level Transformative Responsibility Continuum and evaluated against a common set of postwar indicators: civilian protection, displacement, institutional capacity, and political stability. The comparison finds a pattern consistent with FTPI's core prediction: outcomes diverge least from stated humanitarian aims where intervening powers sustain engagement matched to the transformation they cause (Bosnia and, to a lesser extent, Kosovo), and diverge most sharply where high transformation is followed by rapid disengagement or premature transfer of responsibility (Iraq, Libya, and Afghanistan). Syria, where Western involvement was comparatively limited and indirect, serves as a boundary-testing case for the theory. The findings suggest that outcome measurement anchored to transformation, rather than to stated intent or legal authorisation alone, offers a more discriminating basis for evaluating humanitarian intervention.

detail.abstract: Ukraine’s expanding mid- and long-range strike campaign into Russia and the occupied territories is transforming the character of the Russo-Ukrainian War. Rather than seeking decisive territorial breakthroughs, Kyiv is increasingly targeting the economic, logistical and technical infrastructure that sustains Russia’s offensive capacity. Its strike architecture now extends from the battlefield rear to Russia’s strategic hinterland, over 2,000 km inside Russia. This shift creates continuous pressure across Russia’s entire war-support system, and imposes growing material and social costs on Moscow, forcing it to disperse scarce air-defence assets, protect critical infrastructure across vast territory and absorb mounting economic disruption. The Kremlin’s emerging reaction could develop along three pathways: First, a new equilibrium sought through ad hoc adaptation to the new situation via temporary absorption of hardship, rationing of resources and substitution of domestic production with imports. Currently, this is Moscow’s major approach. Second, a moderation strategy would mean a scaling-down of warfare intensity and negotiation demands once Moscow realises that the country needs at least a temporary ceasefire – a threshold that has not yet been reached. Third, an escalatory response would mean increased terror tactics against Ukrainian cities, hybrid attacks on Europe and nuclear signalling. This reaction is already manifest, among other things, in the mass bombardment of Kyiv in early July 2026. These three scenarios are not necessarily ‘either-or’; they could be pursued sequentially or even in parallel. The Duma elections in September 2026 will influence the timing of the Kremlin’s domestic reaction. Softer methods might be used before the pseudo-vote, followed by austerity measures, increased repression and mass conscription after.

detail.abstract:
Purpose-This research contextually focuses on the financial industry in one of Africa's largest economies. Nigerian financial sector needs to evolve with advanced anti-fraud innovations such as forensic accounting/investigation that will place the institutions steps ahead of the criminals. These innovations will positively impact their fraud prevention, detection and mitigations measures and will boost the confidence of the customer in their services. This study aims to investigate the outcomes of adoption of forensic accounting practices among financial institutions in Nigeria by examining the influence of adoption decision on fraud prevention, fraud detection and fraud mitigation. 

Design/methodology/approach-The study utilises a mixed method approach (survey questionnaire and interviews). The unit of analysis is at the level of an organisation and purposive sampling is used to collect data from Chief Executive Officers, Directors of Finance, Chief Financial Officers, Chief Compliance Officers, Heads of Fraud Investigation Departments and Internal Auditors in the Nigerian financial industry. While the quantitative data were analysed using the partial least square structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM), the qualitative date were analysed using deductive thematic analysis. 

Findings-This study found that the adoption of forensic accounting practices significantly influenced fraud prevention, fraud detection and fraud mitigation in positive directions. Additionally, the study concludes that adoption of forensic accounting has the strongest positive effect on fraud prevention in comparison to its effect on fraud detection and fraud mitigation. The findings significantly differentiated the forensic accounting procedures during fraud prevention, detection and mitigation. 

Research limitations/implications-The limitations of this study include inadequacy of sample size and representativeness of the entire Nigerian Financial Industry. This was due to unfriendly attitude of the financial institutions towards research students. It was a herculean task getting the participants to complete the questionnaire because many of them complained that the questionnaire was too voluminous. The findings of this study have implications for those charged with governance in financial institutions, regulatory bodies, professional bodies, government bodies and other relevant institutions in understanding the importance of forensic accounting and its relevance in fraud management. 

Originality/value-To the best of this researcher's knowledge, there has been no study conducted to investigate the three likely outcomes of adoption of forensic accounting practices in the context of the Nigerian Financial Sector while utilising a mixed method approach. This study significantly distinguishes among the three key activities and procedures of fraud prevention, fraud detection and fraud mitigation when applying forensic accounting expertise.

title: From Causal Factor Investing to Causal Factor Discovery: Evolving a Neuro-symbolic World Model of the Market
affiliations: aiXplain Inc.

detail.title: From Causal Factor Investing to Causal Factor Discovery: Evolving a Neuro-symbolic World Model of the Market
detail.abstract: Quantitative factor strategies routinely excel in backtests and disappoint in production: the flagship live multifactor index earned a Sharpe ratio statistically indistinguishable from zero over seventeen years. Finance research has recently produced a sharp explanation. Selecting factors by how well they fit past returns provably favors the wrong models: the winning specification looks better on every conventional metric, yet it mistakes association for causation and its estimate of the factor's payoff can carry the wrong sign. Machine learning has independently reached the same diagnosis: systems trained to predict are not thereby systems that understand; discovery requires explicit, reusable mechanisms. Both literatures specify the missing artifact-a system that discovers causal structure instead of fitting associations-and both state that none yet exists. We present one, running, in markets. An evolutionary loop autonomously writes and tests small closed-form formulas over market data, admitting a formula only if it improves the model's ability to predict the market's own next state-the features forecasting the features-never for fitting returns in sample. The result is a world model of 151 human-readable equations with zero learned feature weights, its audited core organized into 28 economic factor families. Its inter-family dynamics form a causal graph that reappears almost unchanged when refit on a different country's market (95% interval on the edge correlation: 0.90-0.92) while the factor-to-return mapping does not (interval-0.17 to 0.71, i.e. consistent with no relation at all): the mechanism travels; alpha-the excess return a strategy earns-is local. The system passes, for the first time on discovered factors, the complete seven-step causal research protocol of López de Prado-including the collider audit, a test for variables contaminated by the very returns they are meant to explain, which commercial factor models fail-and its invariant core transfers to a new market at 80% strength with six months of local data. For AI, it is a working instance of the "mechanistic world model" recently called for by Schölkopf and colleagues.

title: Asset Efficiency, Capital Structure, and Network Ownership as Determinants of Private Hospital Financial Performance: Evidence from Georgia
affiliations: Caucasus University and Caucasus University

detail.title: Asset Efficiency, Capital Structure, and Network Ownership as Determinants of Private Hospital Financial Performance: Evidence from Georgia
detail.abstract: Introduction: The financial strength of private hospitals depends not only on the size of their asset base but also on their ability to convert available capacity into operating returns and usable cash. This issue is particularly relevant in Georgia, where hospital provision is predominantly private, infrastructure expansion has been substantial, and diagnosis-related group (DRG)-based reimbursement has increased the financial importance of cost efficiency and asset utilization. Objective: To identify the financial determinants of performance among private multiprofile hospitals in Georgia during 2021–2024, focusing on asset utilization, fixed-asset intensity, leverage, liquidity, operating cash flow, and network ownership. Methods: A quantitative panel-data study was conducted using the audited financial statements of 33 first- and second-category private hospitals. The balanced panel comprised 132 hospital-year observations. Five hypotheses were tested using fixed-effects and Mundlak-corrected random-effects regression models with hospital-clustered robust standard errors. Return on assets (ROA) was the principal performance measure, supplemented by EBITDA margin, operating profit margin, and net profit margin to capture specific financial mechanisms. Results: Hospital size and asset turnover were the most consistent positive determinants of financial performance. Asset turnover showed a particularly strong positive association with EBITDA margin. Higher leverage was negatively associated with ROA and net profit margin, indicating pressure on final profitability. Fixed-asset intensity had no independent significant effect on performance; however, its interaction with asset turnover was negative and significant, suggesting that the benefits of asset utilization diminish in hospitals with more fixed-asset-intensive structures. Operating cash flow relative to total assets was more informative than the current ratio as a predictor of performance. The performance gap between network-owned and independent hospitals widened during the later years of the study period. Conclusion: The financial performance of Georgian private hospitals is determined more by the effective utilization of assets and the generation of operating cash flow than by the size of the asset base or conventional liquidity measures alone. Asset turnover and fixed-asset intensity should therefore be interpreted jointly. The findings also indicate that leverage and ownership structure have increasingly important implications for hospital profitability.

title: Cost-Recovery of Grid-Scale Battery Energy Storage Systems in China’s Evolving Electricity Market
affiliations: , 3rdRail Inc., , University of California, Berkeley - Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (Berkeley Lab), CUNY - Baruch College and University of California Berkeley

detail.title: Cost-Recovery of Grid-Scale Battery Energy Storage Systems in China’s Evolving Electricity Market
detail.abstract: Grid-scale battery energy storage systems (BESS) are playing an increasingly critical role in supporting renewable integration and power system flexibility in China’s ongoing electricity market, yet whether emerging market mechanisms can provide sufficient revenues to sustain large-scale storage investment remains uncertain. Here we develop a two-stage mixed-integer optimization framework in which a representative 50 MW/100 MWh BESS acts as a price-taker in energy markets and a price-maker in regulation markets. Applying it to nine province-year cases across Shandong, Guangdong, and Shanxi from 2022 to 2024, we evaluate whether revenues from energy and regulation markets, combined with capacity payments, can support cost recovery. Under baseline conditions of 80% participation rate and 5% forecast error, co-optimizing participation in day-ahead and real-time markets raises revenue by $30–78/kW-yr relative to sequential strategies. Energy-market revenue alone can recover the annualized capital cost of $68.06/kW-yr in four of nine cases, although profit margins narrow through 2022–2024 and disappear in lower-volatility markets such as Guangdong. The newly introduced capacity payment ($8.96/kW-yr) lifts total revenue to $56–149/kW-yr and enables cost recovery in seven of nine cases, but it remains insufficient for the weakest case. The current mileage-only regulation tariff contributes little ($2–5/kW-yr). Replacing it with a two-part tariff at a 20% price-cost margin (i.e., Lerner index of 0.20) adds an additional $43–62/kW-yr and enables cost recovery in all nine cases, with results remaining robust across margins of 10–30%. Our findings show that the economic viability of grid-scale BESS in China is determined primarily by the energy market, while the capacity payment provides an important but limited complement, and regulation revenues remain constrained. Market reforms that move beyond the mileage-only regulation tariff by properly valuing both regulation capability and mileage could close the remaining cost-recovery gap, accelerate BESS deployment, and support the transition to a reliable low-carbon power system.

title: This Wreckage: Gary Numan and the Expansion of Dystopia
affiliations: University of Puget Sound

detail.title: This Wreckage: Gary Numan and the Expansion of Dystopia
detail.abstract: Gary Numan's early recordings imagined technological innovation and social deterioration not as opposing possibilities but as features of the same future. Emerging from the political and economic crisis of late-1970s Britain, the machine-governed cities of Replicas, The Pleasure Principle, and Telekon shared a dystopian grammar with British science fiction: advanced systems continued to function while the social order surrounding them decayed. This article follows that grammar beyond its original setting. Numan's commercial decline coincided with the absorption of electronic estrangement into mainstream pop, while his later canonization by American industrial musicians returned his early work in a heavier but increasingly familiar form. Drawing on Mark Fisher's accounts of the eerie, hauntology, capitalist realism, and the slow cancellation of the future, the article distinguishes dystopia experienced as formal rupture from dystopia stabilized as genre convention. Numan's later albums extend the same structure from technological alienation to ecological collapse. Savage and Intruder relocate crisis from the declining British state to a damaged planet, narrowing the distance between speculative catastrophe and ordinary political experience. Numan's chronology thereby traces an expansion of dystopian consciousness: from the room, park, and car to industrial globalization and the climate itself.

title: When Does Reinforcement Learning Improve upon Estimate-Then-Plug-In for Portfolio Selection?
affiliations: , The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - Department of Systems Engineering & Engineering Management and

detail.title: When Does Reinforcement Learning Improve upon Estimate-Then-Plug-In for Portfolio Selection?
detail.abstract: We examine the relationship between reinforcement learning and estimate-then-plug-in methods for dynamic portfolio selection. We show that, given finite, discretely observed stock prices, a plug-in method that estimates parameters and computes the optimal strategy under a geometric Brownian motion specification is equivalent to a particular offline q-learning algorithm trained on the same dataset, provided that the true data-generating process has continuous paths-even when the specification is otherwise misspecified. This equivalence, however, breaks down in the presence of jumps. Simulations and empirical tests show that reinforcement learning outperforms plug-in methods under jumps, model misspecification, or market nonstationarity, possibly because reinforcement learning learns decision rules directly rather than an unnecessary full model.

title: Modeling and Optimizing Endogenous Consumer Acquisition in Live-Streaming Commerce
affiliations: Zhejiang University, Zhejiang University - School of Management, Lanzhou University and Nanyang Technological University

detail.title: Modeling and Optimizing Endogenous Consumer Acquisition in Live-Streaming Commerce
detail.abstract: Live-streaming commerce-an emerging and immersive business model-thrives on real-time interactions between streamers and consumers. This paper investigates a critical yet understudied phenomenon within this ecosystem: a streamer's follower base is endogenous to promotional activities. We address the resulting joint pricing and traffic investment problem by proposing two parsimonious choice models-the EMMNL and GEMMNL-that characterize how pricing and traffic investments influence follower accumulation. We formulate the joint pricing and traffic investment problem with endogenous follower size as a non-convex program. By quantifying the marginal value of acquiring consumers, we derive the optimal traffic investment policy and design a visual decision aid to guide traffic investment decisions. This analysis further reduces the joint problem to a pricing subproblem with traffic investment decisions fixed, for which we develop tractable solution methods. Under the EMMNL model, the pricing subproblem can be reformulated as a univariate program, whereas under the GEMMNL model, we design a Fully Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme (FPTAS). A case study calibrated with real-world data shows that treating follower size as exogenous increases out-of-sample prediction error and can cause a 38.75% profit loss. Our analysis yields several key insights: (i) A modest 12% reduction in procurement cost can nearly double total profits, explaining the prevalence of low-cost, low-price products in live-streaming commerce; (ii) Although followers comprise only 14.26% of the consumer base, their revenue contribution rivals that of non-followers, highlighting their outsized economic value; (iii) The short-term marginal value of acquiring a follower exceeds that of acquiring a non-follower, yet this relationship reverses in the long run-implying a strategic pivot: invest in follower acquisition for short-term gains, and in non-follower acquisition for sustained long-term growth.

detail.abstract: Climate change and increasing disaster risks continue to challenge the capacity of educational institutions to sustain safe, equitable, and uninterrupted learning environments. While existing disaster risk reduction initiatives in schools have improved preparedness mechanisms, limited attention has been given to the role of school governance as an integrated system that connects leadership, policy implementation, stakeholder collaboration, resource management, learning continuity, and organizational resilience. This study aims to develop and validate a Climate-Resilient School Governance Model for Sustainable Educational Management in Disaster-Prone Public Schools. The study will employ a sequential exploratory mixed-methods research design. The qualitative phase will explore the experiences, practices, and challenges of key educational stakeholders through interviews, focus group discussions, and document analysis. The emerging themes will serve as the foundation for developing the proposed governance model and research instrument. The quantitative phase will validate the model through survey data collected from school administrators, teachers, disaster risk reduction coordinators, and relevant community stakeholders. Data analysis will involve descriptive statistics, content validity assessment, reliability testing, exploratory factor analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, and structural equation modeling. The study is expected to generate an empirically validated governance model explaining how climate-resilient leadership, governance structures, stakeholder partnerships, resource management, and learning continuity mechanisms contribute to organizational resilience and sustainable educational management. The proposed model will provide educational leaders and policymakers with an evidence-based framework for strengthening school resilience in climatevulnerable communities. The study contributes to educational management literature by 2 integrating disaster governance, sustainability, and organizational resilience perspectives into a unified model applicable to disaster-prone educational settings.

title: When Timestamp Rounding Changes Bottleneck Rankings

detail.title: When Timestamp Rounding Changes Bottleneck Rankings
detail.abstract: Manufacturing event logs often record activity starts and completions on a coarse time grid. A grid that is adequate for trace visualization may be inadequate for ranking stations by mean activity duration. This paper isolates that measurement effect in a transparent synthetic five-station flow line. Four hundred latent logs are paired with 1-, 5-, and 10-minute rounded views using common random numbers. Direct ranking changes the top station in 4.5%, 19.0%, and 30.25% of the paired logs, respectively. At 10 minutes, the mean absolute error in case span is 3.331 minutes and 35.32% of recorded activities have zero duration. A local constrained-jitter procedure is then used to report a probability set instead of forcing a total ranking. At the 10-minute grid it makes a definitive declaration in 7.25% of logs, while wrong definitive declarations occur in 0.25% and the reported set covers the latent top station in 98.50%. The procedure functions as an ambiguity diagnostic rather than a reconstruction of lost timestamps. Sensitivity experiments show that larger logs and clearer station separation reduce reversals, whereas near ties and coarse grids are failure boundaries. The computational evidence targets the modeled setting and supports a practical rule: preserve the finest available timestamps and attach an ambiguity report whenever operational rankings are derived from rounded event data.

title: Financial Civil Death Before Conviction: Liberty, Economic Exclusion, and the Constitutional Limits of Debanking

detail.title: Financial Civil Death Before Conviction: Liberty, Economic Exclusion, and the Constitutional Limits of Debanking

keywords: and the Constitutional Limits of Debanking

detail.abstract:
This article develops the concept of financial civil death before conviction to describe a condition in which individuals are excluded from essential financial infrastructure prior to any criminal conviction or formal adjudication of wrongdoing. In modern financialized economies, access to banking systems functions as a gateway condition for economic participation, enabling individuals to receive wages, secure housing, access credit, and engage in digital commerce.

The article argues that contemporary debanking practices—while formally grounded in private contractual discretion and regulatory compliance regimes—may produce exclusionary effects that are functionally analogous to historical doctrines of civil death, banishment, and legal-social exclusion. However, unlike traditional forms of legal exclusion, modern financial exclusion operates through infrastructural dependency rather than formal status deprivation.

Drawing on legal history, constitutional theory, financial regulation, and socio-legal scholarship, the article traces the evolution of exclusion from territorial and status-based systems to contemporary infrastructural systems governed through AML/KYC frameworks and risk-based financial governance. It further examines the hybrid nature of modern banking institutions, which operate as private actors executing public regulatory functions.

The article concludes that pre-conviction financial exclusion raises unresolved constitutional questions concerning liberty, dignity, procedural fairness, and proportionality in modern financial systems.

title: Strategic Governance as a Service: More Governance Has Not Produced Better Governance

detail.title: Strategic Governance as a Service: More Governance Has Not Produced Better Governance
detail.abstract:
Global spending on governance, risk and compliance runs at roughly USD 72 billion a year, growing above 13 per cent. The frequency and severity of governance failure has not fallen. Boeing, Wirecard, Silicon Valley Bank, Credit Suisse and the Post Office each operated with a board, an audit committee, an internal audit function, external auditors and a regulator. In each case all five layers were present, and all five failed. This paper names that contradiction the Governance Paradox and argues that it has an identifiable cause and a structural remedy.

The cause is three defects in how oversight is delivered. Boards engage with risk episodically, on quarterly reporting cycles that risk itself does not respect, so they see the risk environment as it stood at the last reporting date. Board decision-making is structurally biased toward consensus over resilience, a bounded-rationality problem compounded by the decision noise Kahneman, Sibony and Sunstein document. And no permanent function holds an explicit mandate to challenge assumptions before they fail. Internal audit allocates 75 per cent of its capacity to routine assurance (IIA Vision 2035), and 73 per cent of second-line risk functions report funding constraints on emerging-risk identification.

The paper tests these defects against five extended case studies and against the empirical record of 669 listed companies in Germany, Austria and Switzerland (Hunziker et al., 2025), in which 32 per cent suffered at least one severe crisis between 2018 and 2024. Strategy and external risk drove more than 80 per cent of those events; preventable internal risk accounted for 19.2 per cent. Affected firms recovered to approximately 103 per cent of pre-crisis value after 24 months while benchmark indices reached 115 per cent, a persistent recovery gap of some twelve percentage points that reframes governance investment as value preservation. The paper maps regulatory convergence across the United Kingdom, European Union and United States, including Provision 29 of the UK Corporate Governance Code, the Senior Managers and Certification Regime, DORA, the CSDDD and the Delaware Caremark line of cases, toward oversight capabilities the prevailing model cannot supply.

It then sets out Strategic Governance as a Service (SGaaS): a continuous, adversarial, principal-led governance function retained at board level, with a defined methodology of red team protocol, risk simulation and pre-mortem diagnostic, and a four-tier delivery architecture from diagnostic through to pre-exit engagement. SGaaS complements the Three Lines Model without displacing it, occupying the value gap the model leaves open between mandate and delivered capacity.

The paper makes no claim that SGaaS would have prevented the failures it documents. It claims that the architecture described would have changed the information available to decision-makers, and the timing at which that information arrived.

detail.abstract:
The United States allocates its scarcest defensive munition, the ballistic-missile interceptor, by executive discretion, with no legal rule ranking the claims of Taiwan, Israel, and Ukraine against a finite stock. This paper documents the strategic consequence of that legal silence: the stock has acquired an auditor. Active missile defense publishes its own results; every engagement over Kyiv discloses, within hours, what was intercepted, what was not, and, by implication, what remains.

Open-source evidence from July 2026 shows Russian strike packages shrinking their ballistic component as Ukrainian interception collapsed toward zero, and strike tempo compressing around the defender's resupply rhythm rather than the attacker's production constraint, a pattern the paper weighs against its rival explanations and finds best explained as adaptation to a stock made legible by its own performance. The paper names this condition the Audited Reserve, traces its mechanism, tests it against the July strikes, and states what it demands of disclosure policy, firing doctrine, and allocation law.

title: NP-Hardness of Unconstrained Assortment Optimization under the Exponomial Choice Model

detail.title: NP-Hardness of Unconstrained Assortment Optimization under the Exponomial Choice Model
detail.abstract: The computational complexity of unconstrained assortment optimization under the exponomial choice model is an open question. We resolve this question by proving that both the revenue-threshold decision problem and exact optimization are NP-hard via a polynomial-time reduction from Equipartition. The result holds for rational ideal utilities, nonnegative rational revenues, and a rational threshold, even when the mandatory no-purchase alternative has strictly lower ideal utility than every product.

title: The Impact of Institutional Openness on Export Activities of Firms in China's Digital Service Sector
affiliations: Zhongnan University of Economics and Law

detail.title: The Impact of Institutional Openness on Export Activities of Firms in China's Digital Service Sector
detail.abstract:
This study examines the impact of institutional openness on the export activities of firms in China's digital
service industry over the period 2015–2022. Adapting the Melitz (2003) model of heterogeneous firms, we
develop a partial-equilibrium export decision model in which institutional openness affects firm productivity,
the business environment, and the probability that foreign importers honor their contractual commitments. The
model predicts that institutional openness and firm export experience each raise export volumes, but that the two
act as substitutes: because both operate by reducing a firm's exposure to opportunistic trading partners, the
marginal contribution of institutional openness declines as export experience accumulates. We test these
predictions using a panel of A-share listed digital service firms, with institutional openness measured by a
bilateral index constructed from the OECD Digital Services Trade Restrictiveness Index. Institutional openness
is associated with significantly higher export volumes, and the estimated interaction between openness and
export experience is negative, as the model implies. The response is strongest among small and young firms and
is statistically indistinguishable from zero among mature firms; firms of all three ownership types respond
positively. The sign pattern is preserved under Tobit and PPML estimation and for two- and three-period lags of
institutional openness. Because institutional openness varies only at the national-annual level, we interpret the
estimates as conditional associations rather than causal effects. These results characterize a period of regulator convergence in digitally delivered services, and we discuss why they should not be extrapolated to the post-
2022 environment.

title: AI by Africa, for Africa: Mobilising African Capital for Digital Sovereignty

detail.title: AI by Africa, for Africa: Mobilising African Capital for Digital Sovereignty
detail.abstract: Economic gaps between countries in the Global North and Africa characterise sovereign Artificial Intelligence development as a resource problem. This tension exposes the continent to dynamics that exceed old dependencies, reaching farther to reframe key and sometimes immutable aspects of social life, wellbeing, business and identity in extrapolations based on foreign data. The parallel impact of this trend is failure to capture the exponential economic benefits that Artificial Intelligence development represents for the regional economy. Given the prevalence of low and prohibitive capital allocation to Africa, despite its significant share of the global population, the paper makes a case for the mobilisation of local financial alternatives for the realisation of its AI ambitions. It further argues for the adoption of industrial clusters as effective strategies for derisking investment, pooling resources and catalysing growth.

title: The Innovation Radar 2.0 A Framework for Measuring and Diagnosing Business Innovation

detail.title: The Innovation Radar 2.0 A Framework for Measuring and Diagnosing Business Innovation
detail.abstract: Innovation sits at the top of the agenda for all CEOs. Yet most firms cannot say where they innovate, whether that pattern serves their strategy, or how far practice has drifted from intent. This paper presents the Innovation Radar 2.0, a framework for mapping, diagnosing, and prescribing innovation strategy. It descends from the original Innovation Radar (Sawhney, Wolcott, and Arroniz 2006), which mapped twelve dimensions of business innovation, and extends it in two ways. Beneath the dimensions sits a substrate of purpose, culture, and leadership, rated green, yellow, or red, that gates the returns on everything above it. Above them sits a ground truth: the firm's stated strategy is translated into a target innovation profile, the actual profile is measured against it, and the distance between the two is read as innovation strategy drift. The result is a complete innovation control system. It makes the ground truth financial as well as strategic, testing whether the innovation budget is consistent with the growth ambition before any diagnosis is issued. It translates prescriptions into profit-and-loss terms through innovation elasticity, the rate at which improvement on a dimension converts into financial results. It adds a generative stage that produces a portfolio of fifteen to twenty scored innovation plays, screened against the strategy. And it introduces an evidence protocol that makes scores drawn from public information auditable from the citations they carry. Three case studies show the framework in action: an end-to-end worked example for a synthetic company, an application to Zebra Technologies, and a comparative reading of Anthropic and OpenAI.

title: Where Do Tariff Shocks Propagate? Evidence on Production, Prices, and Shipments from Section 301 China Tariffs

detail.title: Where Do Tariff Shocks Propagate? Evidence on Production, Prices, and Shipments from Section 301 China Tariffs
